## Low-/negative-pressure hydrocephalus — overview and executive summary

### What the entity is

Low-pressure hydrocephalus (LPH), negative-pressure hydrocephalus (NegPH/NePH),
very-low-pressure hydrocephalus (VLPH), acute low-pressure hydrocephalus (ALPH) and
the "syndrome of inappropriately low-pressure acute hydrocephalus" (SILPAH) are
names for one clinical paradox: **progressive ventriculomegaly with the symptoms of
intracranial hypertension (depressed consciousness, headache, vomiting, cranial
neuropathies, gait failure, bradycardia) while measured intracranial pressure is
normal, low (conventionally ≤ 5 cm H₂O / ≤ 70 mm H₂O) or frankly sub-atmospheric**
(down to −10 to −21 mm Hg in reported cases). Shunts, when present, are patent;
conventional shunt revision or a standard EVD at 10–15 cm H₂O fails because the
ventricular pressure never reaches the valve opening pressure or the drain
outlet. Clinical status tracks ventricular size, not ICP (Pang & Altschuler 1994,
PMID 7808607; Daniel 2002, PMID 12027920; Godoy Hurtado 2023, PMID 37373809).

The modern entity was defined by Pang & Altschuler (Neurosurgery 1994), who
treated 12 shunted patients with ventriculomegaly and ICP 2.2–6.6 mm Hg by
prolonged "sub-zero" external drainage and framed the mechanism as a viscoelastic
alteration of brain parenchyma. Precursor descriptions exist from the 1970s–80s
in shunted patients (McCullough & Fox 1974, PMID 4813717; McCullough 1986, PMID
3491341; Foltz & Blanks 1988, PMID 3343612). Before 1994, "low-pressure
hydrocephalus" was used in Europe as a synonym for Adams–Hakim normal-pressure
hydrocephalus; that literature is retained here as a separate axis so it is not
conflated with the modern syndrome.

### Corpus at a glance

- 231 curated records (1969–2026) from a 1,190-record Europe PMC harvest; 32
  open-access full texts mirrored.
- **Core entity axis: 79 records**, 70 of which name the entity in the
  title/abstract; the remainder describe the phenomenon (symptomatic
  ventriculomegaly with patent shunt and low ICP) without the label.
- Evidence is almost entirely observational: 34 case reports, 24 case series /
  cohorts, 3 systematic reviews (Keough 2021 pooling 195 patients, PMID 32736355;
  Bakmeedeniya 2026 pooling 215 patients from 30 studies, PMID 41525875; Chang 2022
  on Holmes tremor, PMID 35148507), 1 consensus statement (Chinese Neuroscience
  Society 2025, PMID 40734409) and no prospective comparative trial.
- Supporting axes: 50 brain-biomechanics / compliance / elastography papers, 30
  drainage-and-valve technique papers (largely EVD-weaning and programmable-valve
  literature that frames titrated drainage), 14 etiological-setting papers, 30
  adjacent differentials (slit-ventricle syndrome, overdrainage, intracranial
  hypotension, venous overdrainage), 28 historical LPH-as-NPH papers.

### Ten take-home points

1. **Rare, under-recognised, and iatrogenically amplified.** Roughly 200–250
   published cases exist (Godoy Hurtado 2023; Keough 2021; Bakmeedeniya 2026).
   Single-centre incidence after aneurysmal SAH is ~3.7 % (Czorlich 2023, PMID
   37004138); in neurosurgical patients with severe disorders of consciousness
   and ventriculomegaly, 60 % had low- or negative-pressure physiology (Zheng
   2023, PMID 36994490). Almost every patient has had at least one prior
   intracranial procedure (mean 3.0 in Hunn 2014, PMID 24275338; ~3.5 operations
   per patient in Wu 2019, PMID 30611954).
2. **Precipitants cluster into three groups**: (a) a CSF sink outside the ventricles
   — lumbar puncture or lumbar drain, skull-base/cranial-wound CSF leak,
   pseudomeningocele, over-draining cyst or spinal shunt; (b) parenchymal
   "softening" — SAH/IVH, ventriculitis/meningitis, radiotherapy, trauma,
   diffuse injury, long-standing shunting; (c) loss of cranial containment —
   decompressive craniectomy / sinking-flap physiology.
3. **The mechanistic debate has four live models** — viscoelastic/hysteresis
   (Pang; Lesniak 2002, PMID 12617236), poroelastic "boggy brain"/Darcy flux
   (Akins 2011, PMID 21523524), transmantle gradient from ventricle–subarachnoid
   disconnection plus loss of brain turgor (Rekate 2008, PMID 18590387;
   Filippidis 2011, PMID 21800965; Diaz-Romero Paz 2019, PMID 30710718), and
   cerebral venous overdrainage/windkessel impedance (Barami 2016, PMID 27581321;
   Egnor 2023, PMID 37382303; Bateman 2026, PMID 42355921). They are not mutually
   exclusive and the leading reviews treat them as interacting (Bakmeedeniya
   2026; Li 2024, PMID 38688300). MR elastography has shown reversibly low brain
   stiffness during an episode (Olivero 2016, PMID 27198914; Olivero 2021, PMID
   33030603).
4. **Diagnosis rests on the paradox plus a therapeutic test**: symptomatic
   ventriculomegaly, ICP ≤ 5 cm H₂O on direct ventricular measurement, patent
   shunt / failed standard drainage, and improvement with drainage at zero or
   sub-atmospheric pressure (Pang–Altschuler criteria; Duan & Hu 2024, PMID
   38579413; Datta & Tu 2025, PMID 41191101). Imaging shows effaced convexity
   sulci and Sylvian cisterns with disproportionate ventriculomegaly, often
   transependymal oedema despite low ICP, and — in the 2025 Chinese consensus —
   a fourth-ventricular "ball sign".
5. **Temporising treatment is titrated (usually sub-zero) EVD**, set to a target
   hourly output (5–15 mL/h, Hunn 2014) rather than a pressure, started at 0 to
   −5 cm H₂O below the EAM (Owler 2001, PMID 11599454), −3 to −10 cm (Akins
   2011, PMID 21523524) or 5–10 cm below the midbrain (Foster 2016), lowered
   further only as needed (−15 in Godoy Hurtado 2023; −30 in one refractory
   case, Salam 2025), and then raised 1–3 cm H₂O every 3–5 days as ventricles
   shrink and ICP becomes positive (Akins 2011; Foster 2016, PMID 27069743).
   Drainage
   durations of weeks to months are typical (mean 41.9 days, range 2–365, in the
   pooled paediatric series of Chen 2025, PMID 40538927).
6. **Adjuncts that raise ICP or close the sink shorten or avoid sub-zero EVD**:
   neck wrapping / soft cervical collar (Filippidis 2011; Pandey 2017, PMID
   28017745; Bruk 2026, PMID 42732439), Trendelenburg/recumbency (Foltz 1988;
   Dias 1999, PMID 10352418), epidural blood patch for post-LP or lumbar-drain
   cases (Dias 1999; Smalley 2017, PMID 28362957; Vilela 2020, PMID 32712403;
   Suzuki 2021, PMID 35854689; Hoffman 2026, PMID 42224725), repair of skull-base
   or wound CSF leaks (Filippidis 2011; Stevens 2024, PMID 39220674), removal of
   the offending spinal/cyst drain (Ozeki 2022, PMID 34526456; Diaz-Romero Paz
   2019), and — a single striking case — theophylline (Salam 2025, PMID 40418891).
7. **ETV is the main strategy for reducing shunt dependence**: a "significant
   decrease" in shunt-dependent patients with ETV in SILPAH (10 vs 10 patients;
   Hamilton & Price 2012, PMID 22116443); 50 % ETV-only success in the Casado Pellejero algorithm (2022, PMID
   34998487); ETV plus valveless catheter gave 81 % excellent outcomes in 16
   adults, 19 % later needing a valved shunt (Villalonga 2025, PMID 41165379);
   but Foster 2016 (PMID 27069743) found
   no significant shortening of EVD time and in Chen 2025's pooled children 91 %
   ultimately needed shunt repositioning/revision.
8. **Definitive drainage needs a very-low-resistance conduit**: valveless VP
   shunts, programmable valves at the lowest setting without anti-siphon
   devices, "therapeutic siphoning" with non-siphon-control or adjustable
   gravitational valves (Bergsneider 1999, PMID 10520938; Trinh 2013, PMID
   22770726; Funnell 2020, PMID 32989519), shunting into negative-pressure
   cavities (pleura, atrium), valves placed below the clavicle to exploit the
   hydrostatic column (Carrera 2025, PMID 39951714), wide-bore custom
   peritoneal catheters (Galbarriatu 2013, PMID 23904087), active-pumping
   shunts (Kalani 2013, PMID 23380444), improvised ultra-low valveless systems
   (Badran 2018, PMID 30287249) and intermittent reservoir pumping for chronic
   failure (Cheng 2017, PMID 28264586; Kuppler 2025, PMID 40030163).
9. **Outcome is bimodal and set by two things**: speed of recognition and the
   underlying disease. Pooled mortality is ~11 % (Keough 2021); 83 % of children
   but only 49 % of adults returned to their pre-episode baseline; 77.5 % of
   children recovered in Chen 2025; but Wu 2019's 39 secondary adult cases (18
   with CNS infection) had a mean GOS-E of 2.7 and 8 deaths. Post-LP paediatric
   cases are the most benign subgroup (Smalley 2017). Predictors of futility are
   unsealed CSF leak, irremediable ventriculitis and permanently altered
   compliance (Houlden 2018, PMID 30009119; Bakmeedeniya 2026).
10. **The evidence base is fragile**: heterogeneous definitions (ICP thresholds
    of 0, 5 and 7 cm H₂O; NegPH vs LPH; acute vs chronic), publication bias
    toward rescued cases, no registries, and mechanistic claims that rest on
    single MRE or phase-contrast measurements. Every major review from 2019
    onward calls for standardised definitions and a multicentre registry.

## History and nomenclature

### 1. "Low-pressure hydrocephalus" as a synonym for NPH (1965–c.1990)

After Adams, Hakim and colleagues described normal-pressure hydrocephalus in
1965, many European authors preferred the term *low-pressure hydrocephalus* for
the same syndrome — an elderly patient with gait apraxia, dementia and
incontinence, communicating ventriculomegaly and a lumbar opening pressure in
the normal range. The 28 papers on the `historical_lph_as_nph` axis are of this
kind: cerebral blood flow before and after shunting (Greitz 1969, PMID 5359210;
Meixensberger 1989, PMID 2608784), isotope cisternography (Jensen 1970, PMID
5457870; Kulczycki 1978, PMID 683432), overnight pressure recordings that showed
B-waves and plateau waves in "so-called low-pressure hydrocephalus" (Symon 1972,
PMID 4117815; Sjaastad 1976, PMID 1278191), infusion tests (Bozzao 1974, PMID
4408072), psychometric profiles (Rivero Hernández 1975, PMID 1211270) and shunt
series with "disappointing results" (Bannister 1972, PMID 4540544; Singounas
1976, PMID 1250499). Symon's demonstration that these patients have
intermittently *raised* pressure is a reason the term fell out of use for NPH.

These papers are relevant to the modern entity in two ways only: they show that
ventricular enlargement can progress without sustained hypertension, and they
are the source of persistent terminological confusion (e.g. a 2013 case report
still describing "acute normal pressure hydrocephalus" for what is clearly
post-LP low-pressure disease; Preuß 2013, PMID 23715811). The Kuba 2002 gait
study (PMID 11749014) and several 1970s "LPH" reports were retained in the core
axis because their abstracts describe low measured pressure with progressive
ventriculomegaly, but they should be read as NPH-era work.

### 2. Precursors in shunted patients (1974–1993)

- **McCullough & Fox 1974** (PMID 4813717): negative ICP in shunted adults and
  its relation to subdural haematoma — the first systematic recognition that
  shunted brains can run at sub-atmospheric pressure, here framed as an
  overdrainage complication rather than a hydrocephalic state.
- **McCullough 1986** (PMID 3491341): *symptomatic progressive ventriculomegaly in
  hydrocephalics with patent shunts and antisiphon devices* — the essential
  paradox (large ventricles, working shunt, low pressure) stated a decade before
  it was named. The anti-siphon device prevented the shunt from ever reaching
  the sub-zero pressures the brain needed.
- **Foltz & Blanks 1988** (PMID 3343612): *symptomatic low intracranial pressure in
  shunted hydrocephalus* — upright, activity-related symptoms with markedly low
  upright ICP, relieved by recumbency and Trendelenburg; Foltz later designed a
  "zero-ICP" gravity-controlled shunt (ZIPS; Foltz 1994, PMID 8194062).
- **Drake 1993** (PMID 8421544): functional obstruction of an anti-siphon device by
  tissue-capsule pressure — an early mechanical explanation for "patent shunt,
  large ventricles".
- **Pomeranz 1993** (PMID 8333302): feline intracranial hypotension reduces cerebral
  blood flow — an experimental hint that low ICP itself can be harmful.

### 3. Pang & Altschuler 1994 and the definitional decade

**Pang & Altschuler, Neurosurgery 1994** (PMID 7808607) coined *low-pressure
hydrocephalic state*: 12 shunted patients with symptomatic ventriculomegaly, ICP
2.2–6.6 mm Hg, patent shunts, requiring prolonged EVD at sub-zero levels
(most for weeks), with symptoms tracking ventricular size rather than ICP. They
proposed altered brain viscoelasticity — a "softened" parenchyma that no longer
returns to shape under a normal transmantle gradient — and established sub-zero
drainage as the reference treatment. Their four criteria (symptoms of
hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly, ICP ≤ 5 cm H₂O, improvement with sub-zero
drainage) are still used for inclusion (Foster 2016; Villalonga 2025).

Subsequent naming:

| Term | Source | Nuance |
|---|---|---|
| Negative-pressure hydrocephalus (NegPH, NePH) | Vassilyadi 1995 (PMID 7666227), after a spinal arachnoid cyst–pleural shunt | ICP actually sub-atmospheric; implies a transmantle gradient created by an external sink |
| Low-pressure shunt "malfunction" after LP | Dias 1999 (PMID 10352418) | Paediatric, post-lumbar-puncture; resolves with recumbency ± blood patch |
| Very-low-pressure hydrocephalus (VLPH) | Clarke 2006 (PMID 16961147); Houlden 2018 (PMID 30009119) | Refractory subgroup with poor outcome after suprasellar/skull-base surgery |
| Hysteresis / non-linear dynamics | Lesniak 2002 (PMID 12617236) | Mechanistic label; 10 adults, mean ICP 4.8 mm Hg |
| Cortical subarachnoid space / brain turgor model | Rekate 2008 (PMID 18590387) | Reframes as ventricle–SAS disconnection; "compliance" replaced by "turgor" |
| Syndrome of inappropriately low-pressure acute hydrocephalus (SILPAH) | Hamilton & Price 2012 (PMID 22116443) | Emphasises acute deterioration and ETV as treatment |
| Acute low-pressure hydrocephalus (ALPH) | Keough 2021 (PMID 32736355); Czorlich 2023 (PMID 37004138) | Systematic-review label; ICP ≤ 5 cm H₂O typical |
| Chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus (cNegPH) | Kuppler 2025 (PMID 40030163) | Persistent ventriculomegaly after failure of prolonged sub-atmospheric drainage |
| Ultra-low-pressure hydrocephalic state in NPH | Funnell 2020 (PMID 32989519) | Elderly iNPH patients who relapse after shunting and need siphoning |
| Two-compartment / acute "normal pressure" hydrocephalus | Preuß 2013 (PMID 23715811) | Idiosyncratic label for post-LP LPH in a shunted child |
| Low-/negative-pressure hydrocephalus (LPH/NePH, L&NPH) | Wu 2019; Li 2024; Chen 2025 | Chinese-language literature; LPH 0–70 mm H₂O, NegPH ≤ 0 |

### 4. Classification proposals

- **Wu 2019** (PMID 30611954) proposed classifying hydrocephalus by ventricular
  pressure — high, normal, low (< 70 mm H₂O) and negative (< 0) — arguing that
  existing schemes (Oi's multi-categorical classification, PMID 21928018;
  Raimondi's unifying theory, PMID 8194058; Rekate's 2008 definition based on
  points of obstruction) give no management guidance for the low-pressure group.
- **Chinese Neuroscience Society 2025 consensus** (PMID 40734409) defines LPH as
  persistent intraventricular pressure < 70 mm H₂O with progressive
  ventriculomegaly and neurological worsening, adds imaging criteria (effaced
  Sylvian cisterns and convexity SAS, fourth-ventricular "ball sign"), and names
  fourth-ventricular outlet obstruction and altered compliance as candidate
  mechanisms. It is the first formal guideline document on the entity.
- **Lin 2025** (PMID 40826122) places low-pressure hydrocephalus as the second most
  common subtype of "refractory hydrocephalus" after infectious hydrocephalus and
  stresses that management hinges on "identifying and addressing the sites
  receiving CSF".
- **Rekate 2019** "Low or Negative Pressure Hydrocephalus Demystified" (PMID
  31103762) and **Rekate 2021** commentary (PMID 34272587) restate the
  turgor/disconnection view and argue the syndrome is a predictable consequence
  of CSF pathway anatomy rather than a mystery.

### 5. Terminological problems that remain

1. **Threshold**: ≤ 5 cm H₂O (Pang, Keough, Datta), < 70 mm H₂O (Wu, Chinese
   consensus), ≤ 0 (NegPH) and "below valve opening pressure" (Filippidis) are
   all in use; a case at 6–8 cm H₂O with a patent shunt set at 10 is LPH to
   some authors and shunt under-drainage to others.
2. **Acute vs chronic**: ALPH/SILPAH (deterioration over hours–days after a
   precipitant) and cNegPH / ultra-low-pressure NPH (months of refractory
   ventriculomegaly) probably share physiology but differ in urgency and in the
   role of ETV.
3. **NPH overlap**: Funnell 2020 and Trinh 2013 describe shunted iNPH patients who
   need siphoning; Doshi 2022 (PMID 36600762) describes an NPH patient evolving
   into VLPH. Whether "low-pressure NPH" is the same disease as post-SAH ALPH is
   unsettled.
4. **Sinking-flap / paradoxical herniation overlap**: after craniectomy the
   same sub-atmospheric physiology produces sinking flap syndrome, paradoxical
   herniation and LPH, sometimes sequentially in one patient (Bateman 2026, PMID
   42355921; Salam 2025).

## Pathophysiology — competing and interacting models

The central puzzle: ventricles enlarge and compress brain even though the
pressure inside them is not high. Every model must therefore explain either (i)
a *gradient* across the brain mantle that exists despite a low absolute
ventricular pressure, or (ii) a change in the *material* of the brain such that a
normal or low pressure is enough to keep it distended, or both. The systematic
review of Bakmeedeniya 2026 (PMID 41525875) identified four commonly invoked
models — viscoelastic change, transmantle gradients, poroelastic/glymphatic
dysfunction, impaired CSF pulsatility — and treats them as interacting. The
clinician-oriented review of Li 2024 (PMID 38688300) covers the same four under
the labels transcortical pressure difference, excessive cerebral venous drainage,
brain viscoelastic change and the "porous elastic sponge".

### 1. Viscoelastic softening and hysteresis (Pang & Altschuler; Lesniak)

- **Claim.** Chronic or intermittent distension (e.g. repeated shunt failures with
  high pressure) permanently alters the stress–strain behaviour of periventricular
  white matter. Hooke's-law elasticity is replaced by viscous creep: the brain
  behaves like a material that has been stretched past its yield point and does
  not recoil when pressure normalises. A *lower*-than-normal ventricular pressure
  is therefore required to restore shape (Pang & Altschuler 1994, PMID 7808607).
- **Hysteresis.** Lesniak 2002 (PMID 12617236) modelled 10 adults (mean ICP
  4.8 mm Hg) as a pressure–volume loop with hysteresis: the volume reached at a
  given pressure depends on the path taken. Only negative-pressure drainage moved
  the system back onto the low-volume limb; ventricles then stayed small at
  normal pressure. Godoy Hurtado 2023 (PMID 37373809) uses the lung analogy
  (inflation and deflation limbs differ).
- **Evidence.** MR elastography in a 19-year-old with shunted aqueductal stenosis
  showed very low shear stiffness during an LPH episode (Olivero 2016, PMID
  27198914) that recovered to near-normal two years later after a
  *high*-pressure shunt failure (Olivero 2021, PMID 33030603) — the only direct
  human measurement of reversibly reduced stiffness in LPH. Houlden 2018 (PMID
  30009119) argued that recovery of GCS despite fluctuating frontal-horn ratio
  indicates "retained viscoelasticity" and predicts salvageability. Supporting
  biomechanics: brain elasticity changes with ventriculomegaly (Sklar 1980, PMID
  6893601), reassessment of brain elasticity in hydrocephalus models (Taylor &
  Miller 2004, PMID 15212932), MRE stiffness falls in early-onset hydrocephalus
  white matter (Wagshul 2021, PMID 33631603) and rises in NPH with partial
  normalisation after shunting (Streitberger 2011, PMID 20931563; Freimann 2012,
  PMID 21538046; Fattahi 2016, PMID 26542235).
- **Weakness.** Does not explain why the syndrome is so often triggered by an
  acute external CSF sink (LP, leak) in patients whose brains were not
  chronically distended, or why neck wrapping works within hours.

### 2. Poroelastic "boggy brain" — Darcy flux of interstitial fluid (Akins)

- **Claim.** The brain is a fluid-saturated porous solid. When interstitial
  fluid accumulates (transependymal oedema, inflammation, radiation injury), the
  parenchyma loses turgor and its ability to resist deformation; ventricles
  enlarge at low pressure. Sub-zero drainage produces a transient "CSF diuresis"
  (drain output exceeds baseline for days) as interstitial water is pulled back
  into the ventricles along a Darcy flux, after which the brain re-stiffens
  (Akins 2011, PMID 21523524: 9 patients, transependymal oedema in 5 despite low
  ICP, EVD output *fell* as LPH developed and *rose* above baseline during
  sub-zero drainage).
- **Model support.** Poroelastic finite-element models of hydrocephalus (Peña 1999,
  PMID 10414573; Dutta-Roy 2008, PMID 18534602; Chou 2016, PMID 26671218; Kim
  2016 on periventricular lucency, PMID 26274984) show that small sustained
  gradients can produce large ventricular strain when permeability and
  elasticity are altered; Solamen 2021 (PMID 32331966) measured poroelastic
  properties of NPH brains during lumbar drainage. Duy 2024 (PMID 38798141)
  reviews hydrocephalus as "biomechanical instability of the brain–CSF interface".
- **Clinical corollary.** Akins' group used the "sub-zero method" successfully in all
  9 patients and internalised with low-pressure hardware; the model predicts that
  fluid shifts (hyponatraemia, low osmolarity) worsen LPH — consistent with
  Houlden 2018's observation that avoiding fluid shifts helped, and with Pandey
  2017 (PMID 28017745) *deliberately* lowering plasma osmolarity to raise ICP.

### 3. Transmantle gradient from ventricle–subarachnoid disconnection and loss of turgor (Rekate/Filippidis)

- **Claim.** Ventricular size is set by the pressure difference between the
  ventricle and the cortical subarachnoid space (CSAS), not by absolute ICP. If
  the CSAS is (a) disconnected from the ventricles by obstruction at the
  aqueduct, fourth-ventricular outlets, basal cisterns or tentorial incisura, and
  (b) drained to a lower pressure than the ventricles by an external sink (lumbar
  puncture/drain, skull-base leak, cyst–pleural shunt), then the ventricle is at
  higher pressure than the SAS even when both are sub-atmospheric; CSF cannot
  return to the convexities and the ventricles enlarge (Rekate 2008, PMID
  18590387; Filippidis 2011, PMID 21800965; Vassilyadi 1995, PMID 7666227;
  Diaz-Romero Paz 2019, PMID 30710718; Suzuki 2021, PMID 35854689). Rekate
  replaces "compliance" with **brain turgor** — the capillary-bed-dependent
  firmness that normally keeps ventricles small — which is reduced by ischaemia,
  radiotherapy, injury and low venous pressure.
- **Predictions that have held.** (i) Neck wrapping / jugular compression raises
  venous and hence CSAS pressure and turgor and reverses ventriculomegaly within
  hours to days (Filippidis 2011; Pandey 2017; Bruk 2026, PMID 42732439);
  healthy-volunteer MRE confirms jugular compression stiffens brain in
  proportion to jugular venous flow (Hatt 2015, PMID 26045579). (ii) Closing the
  sink (blood patch, leak repair, removing a spinal drain) can abort the syndrome
  without sub-zero EVD (Dias 1999; Vilela 2020; Suzuki 2021; Ozeki 2022; Hoffman
  2026). (iii) ETV, which reconnects ventricle and SAS, reduces shunt dependence
  (Hamilton & Price 2012). (iv) Lumbar–ventricular pressure discrepancies are
  measurable in obstructed systems (Chang 2026, PMID 42218510; Staykov 2011,
  PMID 21273925).
- **Counter-evidence and nuance.** Direct measurements have failed to find a
  transmantle gradient in communicating or non-communicating hydrocephalus at
  steady state (Stephensen 2002, PMID 11904027; Shapiro 1987 cats, PMID
  3598675; Eide 2010 on pulsatile gradient, PMID 20130957), while Conner 1984
  (PMID 6737056) did find one in experimental NPH. Advocates reply that the
  relevant gradient is small, dynamic and only present while a sink is active,
  and that MRI-derived transmantle pressures (Sincomb 2021, PMID 34385144) are
  on the order of Pascals — enough over time in a soft brain.

### 4. Cerebral venous overdrainage, windkessel and pulsatility models

- **Venous overdrainage (Barami 2016, PMID 27581321).** CSF diversion at low
  pressure lowers the pressure surrounding cortical veins and bridging veins,
  collapsing them or increasing venous outflow, reducing cerebral blood volume
  and turgor; the brain "deflates" toward the ventricles. Vilela 2020 (PMID
  32712403) invoked this for post-LP LPH in an adult; Datta & Tu 2025 (PMID
  41191101) found prior jugular/sigmoid sinus thrombosis in a third of their
  paediatric LPH patients and modelled venous thrombosis as a predisposing
  factor; Sainz 2019 (PMID 30474714) showed the mirror image — venous
  hypertension increases turgor and *prevents* ventriculomegaly in infant
  "external hydrocephalus".
- **Windkessel / CSF path impedance (Egnor 2023, PMID 37382303; Egnor 2026, PMID
  41791099).** In a lumped electrical model the cranium is a band-stop filter that
  shunts arterial pulsatile energy through CSF to the veins. Egnor classifies
  hydrocephalus by CSF-path impedance: obstructive = high resistance; NPH = low
  inertance and high compliance; **low-pressure hydrocephalus = high resistance
  *and* high compliance**. Ventriculomegaly is an adaptive response that lowers
  impedance, which is why it can occur at any absolute pressure. Related
  pulse-wave-encephalopathy work (Bateman 2002, PMID 12221445; Bateman 2008,
  PMID 18379767) and pulsatility-driven glymphatic flow (Nozaleda 2025, PMID
  40258946) feed this view.
- **Autoregulatory reset and capillary CSF absorption (Bateman 2026, PMID
  42355921).** In a craniectomy patient who passed through sinking-flap syndrome
  and LPH, phase-contrast MRI showed bilaterally reduced CBF that rose by 26 % after
  cranioplasty and *reversed* aqueductal CSF flow toward the ventricles during the
  LPH phase. Lumped-parameter modelling favoured arteriolar constriction from an
  autoregulation reset over venous compression, and the authors hypothesise
  increased CSF absorption via the capillary bed at low ICP.
- **Unified mathematical model (Wang & Lu 2020 preprint).** A U-shaped ICP–volume
  curve that claims to explain slit ventricles, NPH/LPH and paradoxical herniation
  in one framework; untested.

### 5. Compliance, elastance and pressure–volume physiology (supporting axis)

The 50 biomechanics papers give the vocabulary and measurements the LPH
literature borrows:

- **Pressure–volume compensation** (Czosnyka 1996, PMID 8778261; Czosnyka 2001 age
  dependence, PMID 11235954; Kim 2009 compensatory reserve index, PMID 19240611;
  Gholampour 2022 new definition of compliance after shunting, PMID 35979170).
  LPH is a state of *high* compliance / low elastance: large volume change for
  little pressure change — the opposite of slit-ventricle syndrome.
- **Age and species dependence of viscoelasticity** (Shulyakov 2011, PMID 21316637;
  Shulyakov 2012 acute experimental hydrocephalus, PMID 22806081; Jugé 2016 rat
  obstructive hydrocephalus microstructure and stiffness, PMID 26848844;
  Pattison 2010 feline MRE, PMID 20655045; Dirrichs 2019 infant shear-wave
  elastography, PMID 31464808). Infant brains are uniquely compliant — Rekate
  2020 (PMID 32488353) argues this is why infant hydrocephalus, sinking
  fontanelles and post-LP LPH behave differently.
- **MR elastography in NPH and dementia** (Perry 2017, PMID 28063896; ElSheikh
  2017, PMID 28570101; Murphy 2020, PMID 32058331; Aunan-Diop 2022 scoping
  review, PMID 34687356; Coelho 2022 systematic review, PMID 35488708; Karki 2024
  outcome prediction, PMID 38272572; Hersh 2022 operative applications, PMID
  35933785). Stiffness *increases* periventricularly in NPH and falls after
  shunting — the opposite direction from the LPH case reports, suggesting LPH
  is not simply an extreme NPH.
- **Historical theory** — Raimondi's unifying definition (PMID 8194058),
  Orešković & Klarica's critique of the bulk-flow hypothesis (PMID 21641963;
  choroid plexus role, PMID 28456718), Oi's evolution theory of CSF dynamics
  (PMID 16685545), Li 2008 kaolin models of cortical SAS obstruction (PMID
  18433747), Fukuhara 2001 shunt removal and compliance (PMID 11302655).

### 6. Synthesis: a two-hit, two-compartment picture

The most parsimonious reading of the corpus is that LPH requires **a soft or
low-turgor brain** (hit 1: haemorrhage, infection, radiation, chronic
distension, craniectomy, venous thrombosis, immaturity) **and a pressure
differential that favours the ventricle** (hit 2: an external CSF sink or a
disconnected SAS at lower pressure, or shunt hardware that cannot drain below
its opening pressure). Treatments map onto the two hits:

| Intervention | Acts on |
|---|---|
| Sub-zero EVD | Makes the ventricle the lowest-pressure compartment; unloads interstitial water (hit 2, then 1) |
| Neck wrapping / collar / Trendelenburg / hypercapnia / low osmolarity | Raises venous pressure, CBV and turgor (hit 1) |
| Blood patch, leak repair, removing spinal/cyst drain | Removes the sink (hit 2) |
| ETV | Reconnects ventricle and SAS so the gradient cannot form (hit 2) |
| Valveless / siphoning shunts, negative-pressure cavities, active pumps | Permanent low-resistance path so the ventricle never sits above the SAS (hit 2) |
| Theophylline | Raises ICP in intracranial hypotension — mechanism uncertain, possibly adenosine antagonism and vasoconstriction restoring CSF volume/turgor (hit 1) |

The field has not tested these models against each other; the only human
material-property data are two MRE scans in one patient.
