## Etiologies, precipitants and clinical settings

### 1. What the pooled series say

| Series | n | Population | Underlying hydrocephalus etiology | Precipitant / context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pang & Altschuler 1994 (PMID 7808607) | 12 | mostly adults | shunted hydrocephalus of varied cause | shunt malfunction / prolonged shunting |
| Owler 2001 (PMID 11599454) | 5 | mixed | tumour, SAH, prior shunts | postoperative |
| Lesniak 2002 (PMID 12617236) | 10 | adults | mixed | repeated shunt failures |
| Akins 2011 (PMID 21523524) | 9 | adults (neuro-ICU) | SAH, chronic hydrocephalus, tumour, chronic CNS infection | 4/9 during index admission for intracranial bleeding; 7 days–5 yrs after primary dx |
| Hamilton & Price 2012 (PMID 22116443) | 20 | children + adults | meningitis, post-LP, intraventricular tumours | acute deterioration |
| Hunn 2014 (PMID 24275338) | 8 | adults | mixed | all had ≥ 1 prior intracranial procedure (mean 3.0) |
| Foster 2016 (PMID 27069743) | 16 | adults | mixed | prolonged EVD |
| Smalley 2017 (PMID 28362957) | 29 (30 episodes) | children | tumour, haemorrhage | 11/30 after lumbar puncture; 19 spontaneous |
| Cheng 2017 (PMID 28264586) | 7 | adults | — | VP shunt at lowest setting failing |
| Wu 2019 (PMID 30611954) | 39 | adults | TBI, haemorrhage, tumour resection, CNS infection (18/39) | ~3.5 operations per patient |
| Keough 2021 systematic review (PMID 32736355) | 195 (42 local + 153 literature) | 53 children, 142 adults | neoplasm and haemorrhage most common | 39 % of children post-LP; shunt in situ in 92 % of children and 39 % of adults |
| Casado Pellejero 2022 (PMID 34998487) | 5 | adults | mixed | prior shunt / infection / surgery |
| Czorlich 2023 (PMID 37004138) | 15 of 406 SAH (3.7 %) | adults | aneurysmal SAH | IVH presence and extent; mean onset day 13 |
| Godoy Hurtado 2023 (PMID 37373809) | 6 | mixed | medulloblastoma ×2, TBI with bifrontal craniectomy, craniopharyngioma, leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour, shunted NPH | 4/6 already had mid/low-pressure shunts |
| Zheng 2023 (PMID 36994490) | 41 of 68 DOC patients with hydrocephalus (60 %) | adults with severe disorders of consciousness | TBI/haemorrhage with craniectomy | ventriculomegaly + poor compliance |
| Chen 2025 pooled paediatric (PMID 40538927) | 48 (44 literature + 4 own) | children, mean age 6–8.5 y | neoplasm 71 % (medulloblastoma, astrocytoma 59 % of tumours), haemorrhage 15 % (incl. PHH of prematurity), TBI 8 %, congenital (Dandy-Walker, craniosynostosis, aqueduct stenosis, NF1) | > 50 % had prior surgery; 41 % "spontaneous" after primary treatment |
| Datta & Tu 2025 (PMID 41191101) | 6 | children | — | prior jugular/sigmoid sinus thrombosis in 2/6 |
| Villalonga 2025 (PMID 41165379) | 16 | adults | — | Pang–Altschuler criteria |
| Bakmeedeniya 2026 systematic review (PMID 41525875) | 215 from 30 studies | mixed | TBI, aneurysmal SAH, NPH, postoperative, spontaneous | — |

### 2. Precipitants by mechanism class

#### A. An external or extra-ventricular CSF sink
- **Lumbar puncture** in a shunted child or adult with obstructive hydrocephalus
  (Dias 1999, PMID 10352418; Preuß 2013, PMID 23715811; Smalley 2017; Vilela
  2020, PMID 32712403; Koenig 2025, PMID 41357016; Hoffman 2026, PMID
  42224725). 37–39 % of paediatric cases are post-LP (Smalley; Keough). The
  shunt is patent; the LP creates a spinal SAS at lower pressure than the
  ventricle across an obstructed fourth ventricle/aqueduct.
- **Lumbar or spinal drainage** after SAH or posterior-fossa surgery (Ozeki 2022,
  PMID 34526456; Suzuki 2021, PMID 35854689; Dagnew 2002 acquired Chiari after
  lumbar drainage, PMID 12188966; Staykov 2011 lumboventricular gradient, PMID
  21273925; Bakhshi 2020 lumbar-drain complications, PMID 32711138).
- **Skull-base and cranial-wound CSF leaks / pseudomeningocele** (Filippidis 2011,
  PMID 21800965 — 3 cases after cranial-base approaches, all with documented or
  presumed ventricle–SAS block; Stevens 2024 skull-base leak with tension
  pneumocephalus, PMID 39220674; Smith 2016 posterior fossa pseudomeningocele,
  PMID 29506116; Udayakumaran 2018 leaks after tethered-cord surgery, PMID
  29605699; Bakhsh 2022 LP-shunt tract leak, PMID 35673636; Kumar 2025 extra-axial
  ETV for persistent leak, PMID 41215506).
- **Over-draining cyst or spinal shunts** (Vassilyadi 1995 spinal arachnoid
  cyst–pleural shunt, PMID 7666227; Diaz-Romero Paz 2019 external cyst drain, PMID
  30710718; Marianayagam 2017 trapped fourth ventricle treatment, PMID 28209310).
- **Hemispherectomy with CSF rhinorrhoea** (Daniel 2002, PMID 12027920).

#### B. Parenchymal softening / loss of turgor
- **Aneurysmal SAH and IVH** — 3.7 % of SAH patients; IVH extent is the risk factor;
  aLPH patients later needed permanent shunts far more often (66.7 % vs 17.4 %)
  (Czorlich 2023). Case reports: Wang 2024 with quantitative EEG warning (PMID
  39740216); Weisbrod 2021 angiogram-negative SAH after COVID-19 (PMID 34462697);
  Badran 2018 haemangioblastomatosis SAH (PMID 30287249). Background: Chen 2017
  and Kuo 2021 reviews of post-SAH hydrocephalus (PMIDs 28373987, 34068783).
- **Ventriculitis / meningitis / chronic CNS infection** — 18/39 in Wu 2019; Akins
  2011; Salam 2025; Kuppler 2025. Infection is also the strongest predictor of
  poor outcome (Bakmeedeniya 2026; Houlden 2018).
- **Brain tumour and its treatment** — posterior-fossa tumours in children
  (medulloblastoma, ependymoma, astrocytoma), suprasellar lesions
  (craniopharyngioma; Houlden 2018's four VLPH cases followed suprasellar
  resection), tectal tumours (Chang 2022 Holmes tremor, PMID 35148507),
  leptomeningeal/intraventricular spread (Godoy 2023; Myers 2023), radiotherapy
  (Duan & Hu 2024 list prior cranial radiotherapy as a risk factor).
- **Traumatic brain injury** — Wu 2019; Svedung Wettervik 2022 (PMID 34414834:
  patients with "low-pressure hydrocephalus symptoms" had the best shunt
  response among post-traumatic hydrocephalus patients); Salam 2025; He 2026
  (PMID 42444806).
- **Long-standing shunt dependence** — 81 of the 231 records carry the
  `shunt_dependent_prior` tag; Pang's original series was entirely shunted
  patients; Keough found a shunt in situ in 92 % of children.
- **Sepsis / cardiovascular collapse** (McGovern 2013, PMID 23816322) and
  **COVID-19** (Weisbrod 2021) — single cases suggesting systemic
  inflammatory/vascular insults can precipitate the state.

#### C. Loss of cranial containment
- **Decompressive craniectomy / sinking-flap physiology** — Godoy 2023 case 3;
  Salam 2025; Bateman 2026 (PMID 42355921); Bhatjiwale 2023 malignant oedema
  after cranioplasty (PMID 37680924); Ding 2014 review of craniectomy and
  hydrocephalus (PMID 25252237); Kutty 2018 (PMID 29725175) and Wan 2016 (PMID
  26971294) on managing ventriculomegaly and abnormal flap pressure; Joshua 2011
  papilloedema after craniectomy (PMID 21676532); Zheng 2023 combined
  cranioplasty + shunt in DOC patients. The open cranium abolishes the rigid
  container assumed by Monro–Kellie, so atmospheric pressure acts directly on
  the brain and small gradients translate into large volume shifts.

#### D. Shunt hardware as precipitant
- Anti-siphon devices and gravitational units that prevent sub-zero drainage in a
  brain that needs it (McCullough 1986; Drake 1993; Trinh 2013; Funnell 2020).
- Programmable valves left at high settings after over-drainage complications
  (Marianayagam 2017; Doshi 2022 with raised intra-abdominal pressure, PMID
  36600762).
- Ventriculopleural/atrial shunts and the general risk of negative-pressure
  cavities — Chiang 2001 (excluded from core), Datta & Tu 2025 (used
  deliberately).

### 3. Paediatric versus adult spectrum

| Feature | Children | Adults |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant etiology | Posterior-fossa tumour (71 % neoplasm in Chen 2025), PHH of prematurity, congenital malformations | SAH/IVH, TBI, CNS infection, postoperative skull-base leak, shunted NPH |
| Precipitant | Lumbar puncture in 37–39 % | Usually spontaneous after surgery, drain or infection |
| Shunt in situ at onset | 92 % (Keough) | 39 % (Keough) |
| Distinctive symptoms | Bradycardia, seizures, failure to thrive, vomiting (Chen 2025; Smalley 2017) | Depressed consciousness, headache, gait failure, cranial nerve palsies |
| Course of post-LP cases | Often benign: recumbency ± blood patch; median 4 days of external drainage vs 11 for spontaneous (Smalley) | Blood patch effective in adults too (Vilela 2020) |
| ETV | Rarely sufficient alone; 91 % need shunt repositioning (Chen 2025) | Reduces shunt dependence (Hamilton); ETV-only success 50 % (Casado Pellejero) |
| Return to baseline | 83 % (Keough); 77.5 % (Chen) | 49 % (Keough); poor in infected/DOC cohorts (Wu 2019) |

Infant brain compliance (Rekate 2020, PMID 32488353; Welch 1980, PMID 7373397;
Dirrichs 2019) and the frequency of obstructive posterior-fossa pathology
explain why the paediatric phenotype is dominated by the LP-sink mechanism and
why it recovers more completely.

### 4. Frequency estimates

- Post-SAH: 15/406 = 3.7 % (Czorlich 2023).
- Severe DOC with hydrocephalus: 41/68 = 60 % low or negative pressure (Zheng
  2023) — the highest prevalence reported, suggesting that in this population LPH
  is the *rule* and that recovery of consciousness may depend on recognising it.
- Post-traumatic hydrocephalus: 14/29 shunted patients had "impeded recovery or
  low-pressure hydrocephalus symptoms" (Svedung Wettervik 2022).
- Titanium-mesh exposure after cranioplasty with a shunt: 9/10 had LPH (Zheng
  2025, PMID 39760505; excluded from core but illustrates the association with
  chronic intracranial hypotension).
- Cumulative published cases: ~90 (Strand 2018, 25-year search), ~195 (Keough
  2021), ~200 (Godoy 2023), 215 (Bakmeedeniya 2026). The Chinese consensus states
  incidence is "systematically underestimated" and no epidemiology exists.

---

## Diagnosis, imaging, ICP findings and differential diagnosis

### 1. Clinical phenotype

Symptoms are those of acute or subacute hydrocephalus and are indistinguishable
at the bedside from high-pressure disease:

- Depressed level of consciousness — the predominant sign in the pooled 195
  (Keough 2021, PMID 32736355); may progress to coma with brain-stem signs
  (Hunn 2014 mean GCS rise 4.6 on treatment, PMID 24275338).
- Headache, nausea/vomiting (nausea/vomiting in half of Smalley's children),
  lethargy, confusion.
- Cranial neuropathies (up-gaze palsy, Parinaud's syndrome with tectal
  compression), ataxia and gait failure, urinary retention/incontinence.
- Paediatric-specific: bradycardia, seizures, failure to thrive (Chen 2025, PMID
  40538927).
- Movement disorder: Holmes tremor with triventricular dilation (Chang 2022,
  PMID 35148507).
- **Postural pattern**: symptoms worse upright and relieved recumbent in the
  Foltz/Dias post-LP phenotype (Foltz 1988, PMID 3343612; Dias 1999, PMID
  10352418; Ozeki 2022 headache on head elevation, PMID 34526456) — the same
  orthostatic pattern as intracranial hypotension, which is a clue that the two
  entities share physiology.
- **Timing**: after a precipitant (LP, drain, leak) deterioration occurs within
  hours to days; after SAH the mean latency was 13.1 ± 7.7 days (Czorlich 2023,
  PMID 37004138); after the primary neurosurgical diagnosis it ranged from 7 days
  to 5 years (Akins 2011, PMID 21523524).
- **Early warning**: falling EVD output at unchanged drain height as the state
  develops (Akins 2011); quantitative EEG slowing many hours before clinical
  deterioration, reversing with CSF removal (Wang 2024, PMID 39740216).

### 2. Pressure measurement

- **Direct ventricular measurement is required.** Lumbar pressure may not reflect
  ventricular pressure when the compartments are disconnected (Chang 2026
  lumbar–ventricular discrepancy, PMID 42218510; Staykov 2011, PMID 21273925), and
  in post-LP cases the lumbar compartment *is* the sink. Shunt-tap manometry
  through the reservoir is acceptable in shunted patients (Hoffman 2026, PMID
  42224725), as is Ommaya puncture (Chen 2025).
- **Reported values**: 2.2–6.6 mm Hg (Pang 1994); mean 4.8 mm Hg (Lesniak 2002); −3
  mm Hg (Pandey 2017); −4 cm H₂O (Diaz-Romero Paz 2019); all < 70 mm H₂O and as
  low as −10 cm H₂O (Wu 2019); −5 to +10 mm Hg with excursions to −21 mm Hg
  (Salam 2025); ≤ 5 cm H₂O inclusion threshold in most series (Keough 2021;
  Datta & Tu 2025).
- **Continuous monitoring** (parenchymal or EVD transducer) is used to titrate
  therapy and to document the return of positive ICP as the end-point of
  sub-zero drainage (Pandey 2017; Godoy 2023 — drainage continued "with
  concomitant ICP monitoring at the neuro-ICU"). Background technique papers:
  Chari 2017 intraparenchymal monitoring for CSF disorders (PMID 28799016);
  Toma 2010 continuous ICP to investigate shunt function (PMID 20799857);
  Arroyo-Palacios 2016 ICP pulse morphology predicting EVD weaning (PMID
  27106888); Eide 2012 showing that ICP pulse-wave parameters barely change when
  mean ICP is negative until it falls below −15 mm Hg (PMID 22153319) — so pulse
  amplitude cannot be used to detect the state.
- **The trap**: a *normal* ICP (5–12 mm Hg) in a patient whose shunt is set to 10
  cm H₂O or whose EVD is at 15 cm H₂O is *inappropriately low* for the degree of
  ventriculomegaly and symptoms; the absolute number is less important than the
  mismatch between ventricles, symptoms and pressure (Hamilton & Price 2012;
  Gnanalingham 2004 "14 mmHg: a case of raised intracranial pressure?", PMID
  15201374 — retained as a reminder that thresholds are individual).

### 3. Imaging

- **Ventriculomegaly** out of proportion to the sulci: Evans index > 0.3 (Duan & Hu
  2024, PMID 38579413), rising frontal-horn ratio tracked as the treatment target
  (Houlden 2018, PMID 30009119), third-ventricular width used as the response
  metric (Bruk 2026, PMID 42732439: 13 → 8 mm and 13 → 4 mm).
- **Effaced convexity subarachnoid space and Sylvian cisterns** — the CSAS is
  collapsed because it is at lower pressure than the ventricles; the 2025 Chinese
  consensus makes this an explicit criterion, together with a rounded, enlarged
  fourth ventricle ("ball sign") implying fourth-ventricular outlet obstruction
  (PMID 40734409).
- **Transependymal / periventricular oedema despite low ICP** in 5/9 of Akins'
  patients — counter-intuitive and a pointer to the poroelastic model.
- **Enlarged perimedullary cisterns and brain-stem distortion** after LP-induced
  LPH (Vilela 2020, PMID 32712403), and descending transtentorial herniation
  with ventriculomegaly (Marianayagam 2017, PMID 28209310) — the caudal
  compartment is at *lower* pressure so structures are pulled down.
- **Absent cistern sign** and other LP-shunt function signs are unreliable
  (Kulkarni 1999; excluded).
- **Cine/phase-contrast MRI** documented CSF pathway obstruction in all 20 SILPAH
  patients (Hamilton & Price 2012) and reversed aqueductal flow toward the
  ventricles during LPH (Bateman 2026, PMID 42355921). Radionuclide or contrast
  ventriculography via the EVD has been used to localise the block (Rekate 2008;
  Filippidis 2011).
- **MR elastography** — very low shear stiffness during an episode, recovered two
  years later (Olivero 2016, PMID 27198914; Olivero 2021, PMID 33030603); Strand
  2018 (PMID 28962963) suggests MRE as the tool most likely to give an objective
  diagnostic marker.
- **Sunken flap / paradoxical herniation** in craniectomised patients (Salam 2025;
  Bateman 2026).

### 4. Proposed diagnostic criteria (converging sets)

| Criterion | Pang & Altschuler 1994 | Duan & Hu 2024 | Datta & Tu 2025 | Chinese consensus 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Symptoms of hydrocephalus / neurological worsening | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (progressive deficits) |
| Ventriculomegaly | ✓ | Evans > 0.3 | change in ventricular size | progressive dilation; effaced cisterns; 4th-ventricle "ball sign" |
| Ventricular ICP | ≤ 5 cm H₂O | ≤ 5 cm H₂O | ≤ 5 cm H₂O | 0–70 mm H₂O on ventricular puncture |
| Response to drainage | improvement with sub-zero drainage | improvement with negative-pressure drainage | improvement after CSF drainage | (management criterion) |
| Exclusions | patent shunt | ventriculomegaly from neurodegeneration | — | high-risk history required |

Bakmeedeniya 2026 proposes a "diagnostic and management framework" but the
field still lacks a validated definition.

### 5. Differential diagnosis

| Entity | Shared features | Discriminators |
|---|---|---|
| **Shunt obstruction / high-pressure hydrocephalus** | identical symptoms, ventriculomegaly | ICP high on tap; shunt revision works. LPH: patent shunt at tap/revision, low ICP, revision fails (Filippidis; Hoffman) |
| **Shunt overdrainage / slit-ventricle syndrome** (Faulhauer 1978, PMID 742440; Serlo 1985/1989; Rekate 2008 shunt-related headaches, PMID 18259760; Pedersen 2023 definition review, PMID 36639536) | low or negative ICP, postural headache, subdural collections (McCullough 1974) | ventricles *small* or slit-like; Rekate type-1 SVS is the low-pressure form; treatment is *raising* resistance (anti-siphon, higher valve setting; Gruber 1984, PMID 6726390; Aschoff 1995, PMID 7621479) — the opposite of LPH. Bateman 2013 hypertensive SVS (PMID 23991845) shows SVS itself is heterogeneous |
| **Spontaneous / iatrogenic intracranial hypotension** (Mokri 2000, PMID 11113229; Binder 2002 intrathecal saline for obtundation, PMID 12188967; Samadani 2003 after lumbar drainage, PMID 12493112; Atkinson 1998 acquired Chiari, PMID 9452230) | postural headache, low ICP, sagging brain, obtundation, response to blood patch/Trendelenburg | ventricles small; no ventriculomegaly. LPH is best understood as intracranial hypotension *plus* a ventricle–SAS disconnection that inverts the gradient |
| **Post-dural-puncture headache in a shunted patient** (Koenig 2025, PMID 41357016) | post-LP, headache | check ventricular size — if enlarging, treat as LPH; blood patch carries extra considerations |
| **Normal-pressure hydrocephalus** (historical axis; Khan 2013 overdrainage in iNPH, PMID 23930853; Funnell 2020) | ventriculomegaly with normal opening pressure, gait/cognitive decline | chronic, elderly, B-waves and intermittent hypertension (Symon 1972); improves with *standard* shunting; "ultra-low-pressure NPH" is the overlap zone |
| **Cerebral venous overdrainage** (Barami 2016, PMID 27581321) | after CSF diversion, low ICP | may be a mechanism of LPH rather than a separate entity |
| **Sinking-flap syndrome / paradoxical herniation** | craniectomy, sub-atmospheric physiology, deterioration on LP or drainage | flap sunken, midline shift away from defect; cranioplasty is curative; LPH may coexist or follow (Bateman 2026; Bhatjiwale 2023) |
| **External hydrocephalus of infancy** (Sainz 2019, PMID 30474714) | infant macrocephaly | enlarged SAS with small ventricles from venous hypertension — the mirror image |
| **Ventriculomegaly ex vacuo / neurodegeneration** | large ventricles, normal ICP | no progression with symptoms; no response to drainage (Duan & Hu exclusion) |
| **Tension pneumocephalus with skull-base leak** (Stevens 2024, PMID 39220674) | post-shunt deterioration, leak | air on CT; both may coexist |

### 6. Practical diagnostic sequence distilled from the algorithms (Keough 2021; Casado Pellejero 2022; Hoffman 2026; Duan & Hu 2024)

1. Suspect LPH in any patient with symptomatic ventriculomegaly and (a) a patent
   shunt, (b) a recent LP/lumbar drain/CSF leak/craniectomy, (c) an EVD that
   drains little at standard height, or (d) SAH/IVH with clinical stagnation at
   ~2 weeks.
2. Measure ventricular pressure directly (EVD, shunt reservoir, Ommaya).
3. Confirm shunt patency (tap, shuntogram) rather than revising empirically.
4. Image for the sink and the block: CT for ventricles, sulci, flap, pneumocephalus;
   MRI with cine/phase-contrast for aqueduct/fourth-ventricle outlet patency; look
   for pseudomeningocele, skull-base defect, spinal CSF collection.
5. Therapeutic test: lower EVD to 0 then sub-zero targeting 5–15 mL/h; clinical
   and radiological improvement confirms the diagnosis (Pang/Foster criterion 4).
   The series call the response "rapid" (Owler 2001) but give no fixed
   reassessment interval.
6. Exclude/treat coexisting infection, hyponatraemia and hypocapnia, which
   lower turgor.

---

## Management — acute algorithm, definitive diversion, refractory disease

No randomised or prospective comparative data exist. What follows is the
consensus pattern extracted from the series, algorithms and reviews (Pang 1994;
Owler 2001; Akins 2011; Filippidis 2011; Hamilton & Price 2012; Hunn 2014;
Foster 2016; Smalley 2017; Wu 2019; Keough 2021; Casado Pellejero 2022; Godoy
Hurtado 2023; Duan & Hu 2024; Li 2024; Chen 2025; Datta & Tu 2025; Bakmeedeniya
2026; Chinese consensus 2025), with dissent noted.

### 1. Acute phase — restore brain volume

#### 1a. Remove or counter the sink first where possible
- **Post-LP / lumbar drain**: flat or Trendelenburg positioning; stop the drain;
  epidural blood patch if not resolving in 24–48 h (Dias 1999, PMID 10352418;
  Smalley 2017, PMID 28362957; Vilela 2020 adult, PMID 32712403; Suzuki 2021
  before EVD, PMID 35854689; Hoffman 2026, PMID 42224725; Koenig 2025 cautions
  on blood patch in shunted patients, PMID 41357016). In Smalley's 30 episodes
  post-LP cases needed a median 4 days of drainage vs 11 days for spontaneous
  cases.
- **CSF leak / pseudomeningocele**: direct repair, lumbar drain *avoidance*,
  fibrin sealant (Filippidis 2011, PMID 21800965; Stevens 2024, PMID 39220674;
  Kumar 2025 extra-axial ETV variant for persistent leak, PMID 41215506).
- **Cyst or spinal shunt**: ligate/remove (Vassilyadi 1995, PMID 7666227;
  Diaz-Romero Paz 2019, PMID 30710718; Ozeki 2022, PMID 34526456).
- **Sunken flap**: early cranioplasty (Bateman 2026, PMID 42355921; Zheng 2023
  combined cranioplasty + shunt, PMID 36994490).

#### 1b. Raise venous pressure / brain turgor (non-invasive, hours)
- **Neck wrapping / soft cervical collar / bilateral jugular compression**:
  Filippidis 2011 (all 3 patients), Pandey 2017 (PMID 28017745 — combined with
  Trendelenburg, hypoventilation to raise PaCO₂ and *lowered* plasma osmolarity to
  reverse ICP from −3 mm Hg), Bruk 2026 (PMID 42732439 — two children, third
  ventricle 13 → 8 and 13 → 4 mm within days, both then internalised), Kuppler
  2025 (failed in chronic disease), Rekate 2019 review. Mechanism support: Hatt
  2015 MRE (PMID 26045579). Risks: jugular thrombosis, discomfort, poor tolerance
  in agitated patients; requires ICP monitoring.
- **Head-down positioning / recumbency**: Foltz 1988; Dias 1999; Pandey 2017.
- **Fluid and gas management**: avoid hypocapnia and hyperosmolar therapy; Houlden
  2018 (PMID 30009119) recommends avoiding fluid shifts; Pandey deliberately
  lowered osmolarity. This is expert opinion.

#### 1c. Titrated external ventricular drainage (the reference standard)
Protocol synthesised from Pang 1994, Owler 2001 (PMID 11599454), Akins 2011
("sub-zero method"), Hunn 2014 (PMID 24275338), Foster 2016 (PMID 27069743),
Godoy Hurtado 2023 (PMID 37373809) and the paediatric reviews:

Each step is followed by the source wording it rests on (quotes from abstracts,
or from the full text where marked FT — Foster, Godoy, Salam and Chen from the
mirrored OA XML, Akins and Wu from publisher PDFs). Where the papers do not
state a number, that is said explicitly rather than filled in. Akins 2011 is the
only paper that lays out the sub-zero method as an explicit protocol; Wu 2019
gives no drainage settings at all; Pang 1994, Owler 2001 and Hunn 2014 are
available here only as abstracts.

1. **Establish external ventricular access** — a new EVD or the existing shunt
   externalised; failure at conventional drainage pressure is part of the
   definition, not a step to be tried.
   - Pang 1994: "Seven patients failed to improve with multiple shunt revisions,
     including the use of low-pressure valves. In 11 patients, symptoms and
     ventriculomegaly were not reversed except with prolonged external
     ventricular drainage at subzero pressures".
   - Owler 2001: patients "failed to respond to apparently adequate CSF drainage
     via a functioning shunt (four cases) or external ventricular drain (one
     case)".
   - Foster 2016 (FT), Pang criteria: "(1) Neurologic decline at normal EVD or
     shunt pressures; (2) ventriculomegaly; (3) persistence of ventriculomegaly
     with ICP in the normal to low-normal range; and (4) clinical and radiographic
     response to sub-zero drainage".
   - Akins 2011 (FT) makes the failed conventional heights explicit in their
     inclusion criteria: "(4) clinical and radiographic response to EVD drainage
     at +5 to +10 cm height; (5) delayed neurologic decline accompanied by
     recurrent hydrocephalus despite confirmation of a patent EVD and normal ICP;
     (6) failure to respond to lowering EVD (0 to +5 cm); and (7) clinical and
     radiographic response to sub-zero drainage". Illustrated case 4: "EVD was
     lowered to +5 and then 0 cm without clinical or radiographic improvement."
   - Chen 2025 (FT), 28 paediatric cases with route recorded: "EVD, n (%) 12
     (42.86%) … VPS externalized, n (%) 16 (57.14%) … Ommaya, n (%) 4 (14.29%)".
   - Salam 2025 (FT): "subatmospheric CSF diversion via external ventricular
     drain (EVD) placement or shunt externalization with or without neck wrapping".
   - Catheter site and calibre are not specified in any series; individual
     reports use a frontal EVD (Salam 2025: "a new right frontal EVD").
2. **Lower the drain below the reference point until CSF flows** — start at 0 to
   −5 cm H₂O, go to −10 if needed; deeper settings are reported only in
   refractory cases. No paper specifies a fixed interval between downward steps.
   - Akins 2011 (FT), describing Pang's method: "sub-atmospheric ventricular
     drainage achieved by setting the EVD height below the level of the external
     auditory canal"; their own practice: "sub-zero EVD drainage (typically, −3
     to −10 cm)". Case 6 stabilised "with EVD at −3 cm height".
   - Owler 2001: "a period of external ventricular drainage at heights of 0 to −5
     cm H2O below the reference point (external auditory meatus—EAM)".
   - Foster 2016 (FT): "The EVD was initiated at a subatmospheric pressure, placed
     at a height ranging from 5 to 10 cmH2O below midbrain"; the lowest setting
     in their illustrative case was "−12 cmH2O".
   - Pang 1994: "mean external ventricular drainage nadir pressure of −5.7 ± 3.6
     mm Hg" (≈ −8 cm H₂O).
   - Wu 2019 (FT): "Ventricular pressure was lower than 70 mm H2O in all 39
     patients, and the lowest value was −10 cm H2O" — this is the lowest
     *measured* pressure ("Four patients showed the lowest pressure at −10 cm
     H2O, 2 patients … −5 cm H2O, and 2 cases showed 0 cm H2O in ventricle during
     EVD according to the 2 external auditory canal lines"), not a drainage
     setting. Wu's own management text says only "Precise CSF external drainage
     even at a subzero level" and cites Pang's sub-zero and Hunn's titrated
     methods as "innovative treatments"; no heights or steps are given.
   - Godoy Hurtado 2023 (FT): drainage "at negative pressures which were reached
     progressively to 15 cm below the EAC".
   - Salam 2025 (FT), refractory case: EVD "set to −8 cm H2O", later "−10 cm H2O",
     and at the extreme "set as low as −30 cm H2O for forced ventricular
     reduction"; the drain "was adjusted hourly … by either raising or lowering it
     by 2 cm H2O" to allow spontaneous flow.
3. **Titrate to CSF output, not to a pressure** — 5–15 mL/h is the only explicit
   hourly target in a series; others give a daily volume.
   - Hunn 2014: "titrated to produce between 5 and 15 mL per hour of CSF
     drainage, including drainage under subatmospheric pressure if this was
     required to maintain CSF flow".
   - Salam 2025 (FT), summarising the literature: "large-volume aspiration of
     30–50 mL of CSF and subsequent drainage of 10–15 mL/hr, with a willingness to
     lower drainage settings to less than zero to meet this target"; their own
     goals were 10, 15 and 15–20 mL/h.
   - Daily-volume authors: Godoy Hurtado 2023 (FT) "daily debts around 300 mL of
     CSF"; Pandey 2017 (PMID 28017745) "daily cerebrospinal fluid drainage >200
     mL".
   - Akins 2011 describes the output *signature* rather than a target: "As
     patients entered the LPH state, the ICP remained in a normal range yet daily
     CSF output from the external ventricular drain was reduced."
4. **Expect a CSF "diuresis" when sub-zero drainage starts; monitor ICP if a
   parenchymal sensor is available.** The duration is given only as "several
   days"; Akins attribute the extra fluid to water leaving the parenchyma, not
   entering it.
   - Akins 2011: "When LPH patients were drained at sub-zero levels, daily CSF
     output exceeded baseline values for several days and then receded to
     baseline … When LPH was treated with the sub-zero method, a 'diuresis' of
     CSF ensued." (FT): "During sub-zero treatment, we observed a rise in EVD
     output which we attribute to reduction in ventricular volume and reduction
     in brain extracellular fluid"; sub-zero treatment "will 'wring out' the
     sponge-like cortical mantle … Water will flow from the parenchyma into the
     ventricular system."
   - Foster 2016 (FT): "We, too, noted decreased output during genesis of LPH
     with a significant increase in output during sub-zero drainage."
   - Godoy Hurtado 2023 (FT): "Continuous recording of ICP with the
     intraparenchymal sensor during subzero drainage showed negative pressures, a
     flat recording with no pathological waves, and minimal amplitude between
     systolic and diastolic values, suggesting a very distensible or 'compliant'
     brain."
5. **Response to sub-zero drainage confirms the diagnosis** (criterion 4 above).
   The series describe the response as rapid but do not fix a reassessment
   interval.
   - Owler 2001: "Four of the five patients showed rapid and significant clinical
     improvement … In the fifth patient there was no improvement with low
     pressure external drainage and no shunt revision was undertaken."
   - Hunn 2014: "TEVD resulted in improvement in Glasgow Coma Scale (mean
     increase 4.6, p=0.003), and increases in ICP (mean increase 8.5)"; "Mean
     delay from first negative ICP to TEVD was 1.8 days."
   - Pang 1994: "During external ventricular drainage treatment, symptoms
     correlated only with ventricular size and not with ICP."
6. **Wean upward slowly once ventricles are small and CSF drains at a positive
   pressure; expect weeks to months.** Both explicit protocols use a 3–5-day
   step interval.
   - Akins 2011 (FT): "the EVD was raised in small increments (typically 3 cm
     steps) every 3–5 days. Prior to raising the EVD to a more positive height,
     clinical and radiographic stability was confirmed. If patients relapsed
     during EVD weaning, then the process was repeated. Shunt internalization
     was performed once clinical and radiographic stability was confirmed at
     neutral or positive EVD settings (typically 0 to +3 cm)." "Three patients
     had refractory LPH and were unable to tolerate positive pressure EVD
     drainage" and went to ventriculopleural or valveless shunts.
   - Foster 2016 (FT): the EVD was "incrementally raised 1–2 cmH2O every 3–5
     days"; sub-zero drainage continued "until the ventricular shrinkage was
     maintained at a positive pressure, and a new shunt system could be
     inserted"; "patients required prolonged hospitalizations for protracted
     sub-zero EVD, often on the order of months". Mean time from first
     ventriculostomy to shunt was 73 days (range 14–257) without ETV and 114 days
     (0–236) with ETV, P = 0.16 — means, not medians — and the authors attribute
     the lack of difference to "an inherent bias to perform ETV on patients who
     were refractory to sub-zero drainage". One patient "underwent rapid EVD wean
     (in 8 days) and did not require shunting".
   - Pang 1994: sub-zero drainage "for a mean period of 22.2 days".
   - Chen 2025 (FT), pooled paediatric data: "the average number of days of
     external CSF drainage was 41.89 days, with a minimum of 2 days and a maximum
     of 365 days" (n = 28).
   - Wu 2019 (FT): "the time interval from onset to last VP shunt achieved was
     31–3880 days, with an average of 376 days" (29 survivors). Their shunt
     timing rule: "VP shunt should be considered as soon as the ventricular
     pressure rises above 50–60 mm Hg" (sic — almost certainly mm H₂O, given
     their 70 mm H₂O threshold and valve settings), and only when temperature, blood
     count and CSF in *all* ventricular compartments are normal and there is no
     pneumocephalus.
7. **Infection is both a precipitant and a complication of prolonged drainage,
   and predicts poor outcome.** Wu 2019 is the one series that states both
   directions explicitly (though not the phrase "vicious circle"); Salam 2025
   only re-quotes Wu's numbers.
   - Wu 2019 (FT), infection as cause: "blood and infection can result in
     adhesion and block in the arachnoid space, which will hinder the pathway
     between the cortical arachnoid space and ventricle" → transmantle gradient
     → ventriculomegaly at low/negative pressure. Their diagnostic criterion 1
     lists prior haemorrhage or posterior-fossa surgery "especially combined with
     CNS infection".
   - Wu 2019 (FT), infection as consequence: "external CSF drainage with a long
     time course, especially the negative pressure in ventricles prone to
     backflow from the atmosphere, can explain why there was such a high rate of
     CNS infection in our cases"; "it was very difficult to drain CSF externally
     under low/negative ventricular pressure, which was very easy to backflow and
     cause CSF infection". Case 2 developed pneumocephalus "during
     cerebrospinal fluid drainage backflow". Prevention: "Preventing backflow,
     strict aseptic manipulation, and reducing the drainage time were the key
     issues". Zero pressure is classed with NegPH precisely because it carries
     "a high risk of backflow".
   - Wu 2019 (FT), burden: "Eighteen cases were complicated by intracranial
     infections … 46.15%"; 87.5% (7/8) in NegPH vs 35.48% in LPH (P = 0.0149);
     of 8 deaths, "6 patients died from intracranial infections, which accounted
     for 75.0% and were the main reason for in-hospital death"; NegPH mortality
     5/8 vs LPH 3/29 (P = 0.0056); mean GOS-E 1.63 (NegPH) vs 3.03 (LPH).
   - Akins 2011: "Conditions most commonly associated with LPH are: subarachnoid
     hemorrhage, chronic hydrocephalus, brain tumors, and chronic CNS
     infections." (FT): "We hypothesize that underlying inflammatory or
     degenerative changes alter periventricular brain permeability in LPH
     patients, for example, chronic CNS infection or chemical meningitis from
     subarachnoid hemorrhage." Conversely, they saw no infectious harm from the
     treatment itself: "No long-term complications were observed with low
     pressure shunting such as shunt infection or subdural hematoma."
   - Chen 2025 (FT), institutional cases drained via Ommaya for a median of 105
     days: this approach "increase[s] the risk of intracranial infection, and one
     patient ultimately died from intracranial infection".
   - Bakmeedeniya 2026: "delayed intervention, infection, and irreversible
     white-matter injury predicted poor recovery".
   - Salam 2025 (FT): the index case developed refractory NegPH after shunt
     infection ("removal of his shunt" under ceftriaxone/ampicillin).

Dissent: Hamilton & Price 2012 and Casado Pellejero 2022 (PMID 34998487)
prefer early ETV to avoid prolonged EVD; Chinese consensus and Li 2024 (PMID
38688300) recommend EVD/lumbar-cisternal drainage as first line with ETV or
shunt for definitive care.

#### 1d. Pharmacology (experimental)
- **Theophylline** (Salam 2025, PMID 40418891): refractory acute NegPH after TBI,
  hemicraniectomy, shunt infection and IVH; ICP −5 to +10 mm Hg with excursions
  to −21 mm Hg despite sub-zero EVD (as low as −30 cm H₂O), two ETVs and
  ventriculopleural/ventriculoatrial shunts over ~4 months. After 48 h of oral
  caffeine without effect, "two doses of theophylline 200 mg twice a day" via PEG
  (borrowed from post-dural-puncture headache practice) were followed by
  spontaneous drainage at −18 cm H₂O and, on CT 4 h after the second dose,
  "complete collapse of the ventricles to an almost slit-like appearance";
  focal seizures progressing to status epilepticus began 4 h after the first
  dose. Single case; mechanism
  (adenosine antagonism → cerebral vasoconstriction → restored CSF production /
  turgor?) untested.
- **Acetazolamide / diuretics** are contraindicated in principle (they lower ICP
  further); mentioned only as things to stop.
- No other drug has been reported for the entity; the consensus and review
  literature is silent on pharmacology beyond avoiding ICP-lowering agents.

### 2. Reconnecting the compartments — ETV

- **Rationale**: if the syndrome depends on ventricle–SAS disconnection, a
  fenestration abolishes the gradient and may abolish shunt dependence (Rekate
  2008; Hamilton & Price 2012).
- **Data**:
  - Hamilton & Price 2012 (PMID 22116443): 20 SILPAH patients, 10 managed with and 10
    without ETV; ETV produced "a rapid return of normal ICP dynamics and a
    significant decrease in the number of shunt-dependent patients".
  - Casado Pellejero 2022 (PMID 34998487): algorithm with early ETV; 5 patients,
    ETV alone succeeded in 50 %, remainder needed a shunt; one death from systemic infection.
  - Villalonga 2025 (PMID 41165379): ETV in 16 adults, then valveless VP shunt if
    persistent; 81 % excellent outcome, mean KPS gain 56 points; 19 % system
    dysfunction requiring a valved shunt.
  - Foster 2016 (PMID 27069743): 16 patients, ETV did not significantly reduce
    the duration of EVD or shunt dependence.
  - Chen 2025 pooled paediatric: conservative measures and ETV rarely sufficed;
    91 % ultimately required shunt repositioning/revision.
  - Kuppler 2025: ETV failed in chronic NegPH.
  - Kumar 2025 (PMID 41215506): "extra-axial ETV" (fenestration through the
    cranial defect) for LPH with persistent leak.
- **Interpretation**: ETV appears to help a subset — adults with demonstrable
  distal obstruction and preserved SAS absorption — and is a reasonable step
  once ventricles have been re-inflated; it is not a substitute for sub-zero
  drainage in the acute phase and its comparative benefit is confounded by
  selection (Godoy 2023).

### 3. Definitive CSF diversion — minimise resistance, exploit gravity

The permanent shunt must be able to operate at the sub-zero pressures the brain
needs, i.e. the opposite design philosophy to anti-siphon devices:

| Strategy | Sources | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Programmable valve at lowest setting, **no** anti-siphon / gravitational unit | Pang 1994; Akins 2011; Marianayagam 2017; Chen 2025 (most children); Godoy 2023 | Standard first choice; risk of later overdrainage/SVS so needs follow-up and gradual up-titration |
| **Valveless** VP shunt | Villalonga 2025; Badran 2018 (PMID 30287249 — improvised ultra-low-pressure valveless system); Duan & Hu 2024 | Highest flow; watch for subdurals (McCullough 1974) |
| "Therapeutic siphoning" — non-siphon-control valve or adjustable gravitational valve set to permit upright siphoning | Bergsneider 1999 (PMID 10520938: adults improved with siphoning); Trinh 2013 (PMID 22770726: converting to siphon-permitting valve in shunted NPH with LPH physiology); Funnell 2020 (PMID 32989519: ultra-low-pressure state in NPH treated by siphoning) | Applies chiefly to adult NPH-overlap cases |
| Valve placed **below the clavicle** (caudal) to add a hydrostatic column | Carrera 2025 (PMID 39951714); Datta & Tu 2025 cite "shunt repositioning" | Converts body height into negative drainage pressure |
| Shunt into a **negative-pressure cavity** (pleura, atrium) | Salam 2025 (VPleural); Datta & Tu 2025; Chen 2025 (ventriculopleural in refractory children); Chiang 2001 (excluded — positive-pressure ventilation obstructs VPl shunts) | Pleural pressure −5 to −8 cm H₂O in spontaneous breathing; ineffective under mechanical ventilation |
| Wide-bore / low-resistance custom distal catheter | Galbarriatu 2013 (PMID 23904087 — thoracic-drain tubing as peritoneal catheter) | Reduces distal resistance |
| **Active-pumping / negative-pressure shunt** | Kalani 2013 (PMID 23380444 — investigational active shunt in a patient failing sub-zero EVD); background valve-technology literature: Aschoff 1995 (PMID 7621479), Czosnyka 2002 UK shunt evaluation (PMID 12111485), Chari 2014 (PMID 24405071) | Not commercially available; case-level evidence |
| Zero-ICP gravity shunt (ZIPS) | Foltz 1994 (PMID 8194062) | Historical; 56 patients, Foltz's own design |
| **Intermittent reservoir pumping** | Cheng 2017 (PMID 28264586: 7 adults with VP shunt at lowest setting; compressing the pump chamber several times daily improved ventricles in 6/7); Kuppler 2025 (PMID 40030163: scheduled active pressing as outpatient rescue) | Cheap, needs compliance and follow-up |
| Combined cranioplasty + shunt in craniectomised DOC patients | Zheng 2023 | Single-stage restoration of container and drainage |

Sequencing (Godoy 2023; Datta & Tu 2025; Chen 2025): internalise once the
patient tolerates EVD raised to ≥ 0–5 cm H₂O with stable ventricles; if
internalisation fails at the lowest valve setting, consider valveless/negative
cavity/caudal valve; if the patient re-develops LPH after a period of stability,
re-externalise and repeat sub-zero drainage — many patients cycle several times
(Wu 2019: 3.5 procedures per patient).

### 4. Chronic and refractory disease

Defined operationally as persistent or recurrent symptomatic ventriculomegaly
after adequate sub-zero drainage, ETV and low-resistance shunting (Kuppler
2025's *chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus*; Clarke 2006 / Houlden 2018
*very-low-pressure hydrocephalus*; Lin 2025 *refractory hydrocephalus*).

- **Predictors of refractoriness**: unsealed CSF leak, ongoing ventriculitis,
  suprasellar/skull-base surgery, multiple prior operations, severe underlying
  brain injury, permanently altered compliance (Houlden 2018; Bakmeedeniya 2026;
  Wu 2019).
- **Options tried**: prolonged (months) sub-atmospheric drainage; ETV; low-gradient
  shunt; neck wrapping (failed in Kuppler's case); intermittent active shunt
  pumping (Kuppler, Cheng); ventriculopleural conversion; theophylline (Salam);
  MRE-guided timing (Olivero — stiffness recovery may indicate when a standard
  valve can be tolerated); cranioplasty; and, in the DOC population, acceptance
  of a permanent low-pressure system with continued rehabilitation (Zheng 2023).
- **Prognosis**: Houlden's 4 VLPH cases and Wu's infected subgroup had the worst
  outcomes (mean GOS-E 2.7); Kuppler's patient remained shunt-dependent but
  stable as an outpatient.

### 5. Paediatric specifics

- Post-LP cases: recumbency, then blood patch; many resolve without drainage
  (Dias; Smalley).
- Spontaneous cases after posterior-fossa tumour surgery: EVD titration exactly
  as in adults; long durations (up to a year); most end with a programmable valve
  at lowest setting, some with ventriculopleural or repositioned shunts (Chen
  2025).
- Neck wrapping is tolerated and effective in children (Bruk 2026).
- ETV alone is rarely sufficient (Chen 2025) — possibly because absorption at
  the convexity is also impaired by tumour/haemorrhage.
- Outcome: 77.5 % back to baseline; deaths driven by tumour progression.

### 6. What to avoid (from the failure reports)

- Standard-height EVD, standard valve settings or anti-siphon devices in a brain
  showing the paradox (McCullough 1986; Drake 1993; Trinh 2013).
- Empirical shunt revision without pressure measurement (Filippidis; Hoffman).
- Lumbar puncture or lumbar drainage in a patient with a patent shunt and
  obstructive pathology (Dias; Preuß; Ozeki) — or at least anticipate LPH.
- Osmotherapy, hyperventilation, diuretics in a patient with low ICP and large
  ventricles.
- Leaving a skull-base leak or pseudomeningocele untreated while draining
  sub-zero — the two sinks compete.
- Assuming that a "normal" ICP excludes hydrocephalus when the ventricles are
  enlarging and the patient is deteriorating.

---

## Outcomes, prognostic factors, evidence quality and research agenda

### 1. Outcome data

| Source | n | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Pang & Altschuler 1994 (PMID 7808607) | 12 | All improved with sub-zero drainage; most internalised with low-pressure hardware |
| Lesniak 2002 (PMID 12617236) | 10 | Ventricles returned to baseline size and stayed small at normal pressure after negative-pressure drainage |
| Akins 2011 (PMID 21523524) | 9 | Sub-zero method effective in all; internalised |
| Filippidis 2011 (PMID 21800965) | 3 | All resolved after leak repair + neck wrapping/drainage |
| Hamilton & Price 2012 (PMID 22116443) | 20 | Shunt dependence 20 % with ETV vs 70 % without |
| Hunn 2014 (PMID 24275338) | 8 | Mean GCS improvement 4.6; ventricular size reduced in all |
| Foster 2016 (PMID 27069743) | 16 | Prolonged EVD; ETV no significant benefit on EVD duration |
| Smalley 2017 (PMID 28362957) | 29/30 episodes | Post-LP: median 4 days drainage, generally full recovery; spontaneous: median 11 days |
| Cheng 2017 (PMID 28264586) | 7 | Reservoir pumping improved 6/7 |
| Houlden 2018 (PMID 30009119) | 4 VLPH | Prolonged courses; recovery of GCS despite persistent ventriculomegaly in salvageable cases; poor overall |
| Wu 2019 (PMID 30611954) | 39 | Mean GOS-E 2.7 (1.6 NegPH vs 3.0 LPH); 8 deaths (5/8 NegPH vs 3/29 LPH), 6 of them from CNS infection |
| Keough 2021 SR (PMID 32736355) | 195 | Return to baseline 83 % children vs 49 % adults; overall mortality ~11 % |
| Casado Pellejero 2022 (PMID 34998487) | 5 | ETV alone 50 %; remainder shunted; low-pressure state resolved in all treated; 1 death (20 %) from systemic infection; 80 % good outcome |
| Czorlich 2023 (PMID 37004138) | 15 | Post-SAH aLPH → permanent shunt 66.7 % vs 17.4 % in other SAH patients; outcome otherwise not worse than matched SAH |
| Godoy Hurtado 2023 (PMID 37373809) | 6 | 5/6 improved; treatment individualised; ~200 cases in literature |
| Chen 2025 pooled paediatric (PMID 40538927) | 48 | 77.5 % returned to pre-existing status; deaths and poor outcomes due to underlying tumour/haemorrhage; mean external drainage 41.9 d |
| Villalonga 2025 (PMID 41165379) | 16 | 81 % excellent, 19 % temporary improvement; mean KPS gain 56; 19 % needed a valved shunt |
| Datta & Tu 2025 (PMID 41191101) | 6 | All improved with drainage; shunt repositioning or negative-pressure cavities |
| Bakmeedeniya 2026 SR (PMID 41525875) | 215 | Prognosis governed by etiology and speed of recognition; standardised framework proposed |

**Summary**: when recognised and treated with titrated sub-zero drainage, most
patients regain their pre-episode status; mortality of ~10 % and poor
functional outcome in about a quarter to a half of adults is attributable mainly
to the underlying disease (SAH, TBI, tumour, ventriculitis) and to delayed
recognition. Children and post-LP cases do best; infected and skull-base/VLPH
cases do worst. Permanent shunt dependence is the norm (≥ 70 % without ETV, 50–80
% overall).

### 2. Prognostic factors reported

Favourable: paediatric age; post-LP precipitant; short delay to sub-zero
drainage; identifiable and closable sink; retained viscoelasticity (GCS improves
before ventricles shrink; Houlden); clear distal obstruction amenable to ETV.

Unfavourable: CNS infection; unsealed CSF leak; suprasellar/skull-base surgery;
multiple prior operations; decompressive craniectomy with DOC; large IVH burden
(Czorlich); need for drainage at ≤ −10 cm H₂O; chronic course > 3 months
(Kuppler).

### 3. Complications specific to treatment

- Sub-zero EVD: ventriculitis with prolonged drainage; subdural haematoma or
  hygroma from overdrainage (McCullough & Fox 1974, PMID 4813717); intracranial
  hypotension symptoms; catheter blockage as ventricles collapse.
- Neck wrapping: jugular venous thrombosis risk, patient intolerance.
- Blood patch in shunted patients: theoretical risk of shunt tract/lumbar
  complications (Koenig 2025, PMID 41357016).
- Valveless / siphoning shunts: subdurals, slit ventricles — the pendulum swings
  to overdrainage (Faulhauer 1978, PMID 742440; Serlo 1985, PMID 4064018;
  Pedersen 2023, PMID 36639536); Doshi 2022 (PMID 36600762) illustrates
  oscillation between overdrainage and VLPH in one patient.
- Ventriculopleural shunts: pleural effusion; failure under positive-pressure
  ventilation.
- Theophylline: seizures (Salam 2025).

### 4. Evidence quality

- **Design**: 3 systematic reviews of case-level data, 1 consensus statement,
  ~24 retrospective series/cohorts (largest single-centre n = 42, Keough; largest
  pooled n = 215), 34 case reports, no prospective study, no trial, no registry.
- **Definitional heterogeneity**: ICP thresholds ≤ 0, ≤ 5 cm H₂O, < 7 cm H₂O; some
  series include "normal" ICP with failed standard drainage; acute and chronic
  cases pooled.
- **Selection and publication bias**: successful sub-zero drainage and successful
  ETV are over-reported; unrecognised cases (likely frequent in DOC and SAH
  populations — Zheng 2023; Czorlich 2023) are absent.
- **Mechanistic evidence**: mostly inference from treatment response; one patient
  with serial MRE; one with phase-contrast CBF/CSF flow; no direct transmantle
  gradient measurements during an episode; animal models (Shulyakov 2012, Jugé
  2016, Li 2008 kaolin) address hydrocephalus compliance generally, not LPH.
- **Outcome measures**: GCS, GOS-E, mRS, "return to baseline", frontal-horn
  ratio, third-ventricle width — inconsistent and rarely blinded.
- **Language/region**: a substantial body of Chinese literature (Wu 2019; Cheng
  2017; Li 2024; Chen 2025; Zheng 2023; Chinese consensus 2025; Lin 2025) uses
  the < 70 mm H₂O threshold and reports higher prevalence in DOC/post-infectious
  cohorts than Western series — possibly true case mix, possibly definitional.

### 5. Open questions and a research agenda

1. **Definition**: adopt a single operational definition (symptomatic progressive
   ventriculomegaly + directly measured ventricular pressure ≤ 5 cm H₂O or ≤ 70
   mm H₂O + failure of standard-pressure drainage), with acute/chronic and
   LPH/NegPH sub-labels — a Delphi process is the obvious next step after the
   2025 Chinese consensus.
2. **Epidemiology**: prospective screening of SAH, posterior-fossa tumour,
   ventriculitis and craniectomy/DOC cohorts with routine ventricular pressure
   measurement when ventricles enlarge; the 3.7 % and 60 % figures need
   replication.
3. **Mechanism**: serial MR elastography and phase-contrast MRI during and after
   episodes; simultaneous ventricular and lumbar/cortical pressure recordings to
   test the transmantle hypothesis directly; interstitial-water quantification
   (diffusion, T2 mapping) to test the poroelastic model; venous sinus imaging to
   test the venous overdrainage/thrombosis association (Datta & Tu 2025).
4. **Treatment protocol**: standardise sub-zero EVD titration (height steps,
   output targets, weaning rate) and compare early ETV vs prolonged EVD in a
   multicentre registry; define when neck wrapping or blood patch can replace
   drainage.
5. **Hardware**: evaluate caudal valve placement, valveless systems, pleural
   shunts and active-pumping devices head to head for internalisation failure
   rates and overdrainage complications.
6. **Pharmacology**: methylxanthines (theophylline, caffeine) and other agents
   used for intracranial hypotension deserve a formal case series with ICP
   monitoring.
7. **Biomarkers**: EVD output trajectory (Akins), quantitative EEG (Wang 2024),
   ICP pulse morphology (Arroyo-Palacios 2016; Eide 2012) as early-warning tools
   for the transition into the low-pressure state.
8. **Long-term outcome**: cognitive and functional follow-up of survivors,
   incidence of later overdrainage/SVS after low-resistance shunting, and
   whether brain stiffness recovers (Olivero 2021) enough to permit conversion to
   standard valves.

## Key papers — per-paper extractions

Ordered chronologically within groups. "FT" marks papers whose open-access XML
is mirrored under `fulltext/`; the rest were read from Europe PMC abstracts.

### A. Foundational descriptions

**McCullough & Fox 1974** — *Negative intracranial pressure hydrocephalus in adults
with shunts and its relationship to the production of subdural hematoma* (J
Neurosurg; PMID 4813717). Shunted adults run sub-atmospheric ICP; subdural
haematoma is the consequence. Establishes that negative ICP is achievable and
harmful — the overdrainage pole of the same physiology.

**McCullough 1986** — *Symptomatic progressive ventriculomegaly in hydrocephalics
with patent shunts and antisiphon devices* (Neurosurgery; PMID 3491341). Patent
shunts with ASDs; ventricles enlarge symptomatically; removing the ASD or
lowering resistance helps. The paradox stated before it was named.

**Foltz & Blanks 1988** — *Symptomatic low intracranial pressure in shunted
hydrocephalus* (J Neurosurg; PMID 3343612). Upright, activity-related headache
and lethargy; low upright ICP; relief when recumbent/Trendelenburg. Motivated
the "zero-ICP" gravity-controlled shunt (Foltz 1994, PMID 8194062, 56 patients).

**Pang & Altschuler 1994** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalic state and viscoelastic
alterations in the brain* (Neurosurgery; PMID 7808607). 12 shunted patients,
ventriculomegaly, ICP 2.2–6.6 mm Hg, patent shunts; prolonged sub-zero EVD
restored ventricular size and symptoms; symptoms tracked ventricular size, not
ICP. Proposes viscoelastic change; defines the entity and its treatment.

**Vassilyadi, Farmer & Montes 1995** — *Negative-pressure hydrocephalus* (J
Neurosurg; PMID 7666227). Child with a spinal arachnoid cyst–pleural shunt
developing symptomatic ventriculomegaly at negative ICP; postulates a
transmantle gradient from the extra-ventricular sink. Coins "negative-pressure
hydrocephalus".

**Dias, Li, Freimark & Larson 1999** — *Low-pressure shunt 'malfunction' following
lumbar puncture in children with shunted obstructive hydrocephalus* (Pediatr
Neurosurg; PMID 10352418). Post-LP symptomatic ventriculomegaly with patent
shunts; recumbency ± epidural blood patch resolved it. Establishes the
paediatric post-LP phenotype and its benign treatment.

**Bergsneider et al. 1999** — *Beneficial effect of siphoning in treatment of adult
hydrocephalus* (Arch Neurol; PMID 10520938). Adults whose ventricles and
symptoms improved only when the shunt was allowed to siphon — the "therapeutic
siphoning" idea later applied to LPH.

### B. Series that defined management

**Owler et al. 2001** — *Low pressure hydrocephalus: issues of diagnosis and
treatment in five cases* (Br J Neurosurg; PMID 11599454). Five cases; stresses
direct ventricular pressure measurement and drainage at or below zero; first
UK series.

**Lesniak, Clatterbuck, Rigamonti & Williams 2002** — *Low pressure hydrocephalus
and ventriculomegaly: hysteresis, non-linear dynamics, and the benefits of CSF
diversion* (Br J Neurosurg; PMID 12617236). 10 adults, mean ICP 4.8 mm Hg;
ventricles normalised only after negative-pressure drainage and then stayed
small at normal pressure — a hysteresis loop.

**Daniel, Lee & Halcrow 2002** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalic state complicating
hemispherectomy* (Epilepsia; PMID 12027920). Post-hemispherectomy with CSF
rhinorrhoea; ventriculomegaly at low ICP; treated with sub-zero drainage then
low-pressure shunt.

**Clarke & Meyer 2006** — *Very low pressure hydrocephalus* (J Neurosurg; PMID
16961147) and **Houlden et al. 2018** — *Importance of frontal horn ratio and
optimal CSF drainage in the treatment of very low pressure hydrocephalus* (J
Neurol Surg A; PMID 30009119). VLPH after suprasellar/skull-base resection is
often refractory; Houlden's 4 cases suggest recovery of GCS despite persistent
ventriculomegaly identifies salvageable patients ("retained viscoelasticity")
and recommends frontal-horn-ratio tracking, volume optimisation and avoidance
of fluid shifts.

**Rekate, Nadkarni & Wallace 2008** — *The importance of the cortical subarachnoid
space in understanding hydrocephalus* (J Neurosurg Pediatr; PMID 18590387).
Reframes LPH as ventricle–CSAS disconnection with a lower-pressure CSAS and
loss of brain turgor; predicts benefit from ETV, neck wrapping, and closing
sinks. Companion: Rekate 2019 *Low or negative pressure hydrocephalus
demystified* (PMID 31103762) and 2021 commentary (PMID 34272587).

**Akins, Guppy, Axelrod, Chakrabarti, Silverthorn & Williams 2011** (FT, publisher
PDF) — *The genesis of low pressure hydrocephalus* (Neurocrit Care; PMID
21523524). 9 neuro-ICU patients (0.2% of admissions; 4 of 102 SAH patients with
EVDs); LPH 7 days–5 years after the index condition; EVD output fell as LPH
developed; transependymal oedema in 5 despite low ICP. The only paper to state
the sub-zero method as a protocol: response to EVD at +5 to +10 cm, then
failure at 0 to +5 cm, then sub-zero drainage "typically −3 to −10 cm" below the
external auditory canal; wean "in small increments (typically 3 cm steps) every
3–5 days" only after clinical and radiographic stability, repeat if relapse;
internalise at 0 to +3 cm. Output rose above baseline for several days ("CSF
diuresis"), attributed to water leaving the parenchyma (Darcy flux, poroelastic
"boggy brain"). All 9 resolved; 6 programmable valves at lowest setting, 1
valveless VPS, 2 ventriculopleural (the 3 who could not tolerate positive EVD
pressure); 2 relapses; no SDH or shunt infection at 6 months–4 years.

**Filippidis, Kalani & Rekate 2011** — *Negative-pressure and low-pressure
hydrocephalus: the role of cerebrospinal fluid leaks resulting from surgical
approaches to the cranial base* (J Neurosurg; PMID 21800965). Three post
skull-base-surgery cases with leaks and ventricle–SAS block; treated with leak
repair, neck wrapping and drainage; formalises the leak-as-sink mechanism and
neck wrapping as therapy.

**Hamilton & Price 2012** — *Syndrome of inappropriately low-pressure acute
hydrocephalus (SILPAH)* (Acta Neurochir Suppl; PMID 22116443). 20 patients (10
without, 10 with ETV); all had EVD with drainage below zero; cine MRI showed
CSF pathway obstruction in all; ETV "reestablishes communication between the
SAS and ventricles" with rapid return of normal ICP dynamics and significantly
fewer shunt-dependent patients.

**Kalani, Turner & Nakaji 2013** — *Treatment of refractory low-pressure
hydrocephalus with an active pumping negative-pressure shunt system* (J Clin
Neurosci; PMID 23380444). Investigational active shunt for a patient failing
sub-zero EVD.

**Galbarriatu et al. 2013** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalus: a case report and
review* (Neurocirugia; PMID 23904087). Custom wide-bore peritoneal catheter
(thoracic-drain tubing) to minimise distal resistance.

**Trinh et al. 2013** — *Shunt overdrainage or low-pressure hydrocephalus?*
(Neurosurgery; PMID 22770726). Shunted NPH patient with LPH physiology treated
by converting to a siphon-permitting system — highlights the overdrainage/LPH
diagnostic fork.

**Hunn et al. 2014** — *Successful treatment of negative pressure hydrocephalus
using timely titrated external ventricular drainage and a low-pressure
ventriculoperitoneal shunt* (Clin Neurol Neurosurg; PMID 24275338). 8 adults,
mean 3.0 prior procedures; TEVD titrated to 5–15 mL/h including sub-atmospheric
drainage, then low-pressure VP shunt; mean GCS improvement 4.6; first series to
report acceptable long-term outcomes.

**Foster, Zlotnikov & Rekate (Foster 2016)** — *Analysis of low-pressure
hydrocephalus: does ETV shorten time to internalization?* (World Neurosurg; PMID
27069743). 16 patients; ETV did not significantly shorten EVD duration.

**Olivero et al. 2016 / 2021** — *Magnetic resonance elastography demonstrating low
brain stiffness in a patient with low-pressure hydrocephalus* (PMID 27198914) and
*Brain stiffness following recovery in a patient with an episode of low-pressure
hydrocephalus* (PMID 33030603). The only direct material-property data: very low
shear stiffness during the episode, recovered two years later.

**Barami, Sood 2016** — *The cerebral venous system and the postural regulation of
intracranial pressure: implications in the management of patients with
cerebrospinal fluid diversion* (Childs Nerv Syst; PMID 27581321). Venous
overdrainage model for low-pressure states after CSF diversion.

**Pandey, Ali, Vasenina & Prasad 2017** — *Management of negative pressure
hydrocephalus* (Neurol India; PMID 28017745). ICP −3 mm Hg reversed with
Trendelenburg, cervical wrapping, hypoventilation (raising PaCO₂) and lowered
plasma osmolarity — the most explicit "raise ICP medically" protocol.

**Smalley, Spiro & Dias 2017** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalus in children: a case
series and review of the literature* (Neurosurgery; PMID 28362957). 30 episodes
in 29 children; 37.9 % post-LP; post-LP cases: conservative 27 %, blood patch
18 %, drainage in the rest; median 4 vs 11 days of drainage for post-LP vs
spontaneous.

**Cheng et al. 2017** — *Clinical manifestations and treatment of low-pressure
hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt* (Chinese; PMID 28264586). 7
adults with shunts at lowest setting still enlarging; intermittent manual
compression of the reservoir several times a day improved 6/7 — the origin of
the "reservoir pumping" strategy later used by Kuppler 2025.

**Marianayagam et al. 2017** — *Trapped fourth ventricle and LPH* (PMID 28209310)
and **Badran et al. 2018** — improvised ultra-low-pressure valveless shunt after
SAH in haemangioblastomatosis (PMID 30287249): hardware improvisation case
reports.

**Strand, Balise, Leung & Boop 2018** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalus: a case report
and review of the literature* (World Neurosurg; PMID 28962963). 25-year search,
17 articles, 90 cases; argues MRE may become the objective diagnostic tool and
ETV a strong alternative/adjunct.

**Wu, Zang, Wu, Sun, Yu & Hu 2019** (FT, publisher PDF) — *Diagnosis and
management for secondary low- or negative-pressure hydrocephalus and a new
hydrocephalus classification based on ventricular pressure* (World Neurosurg;
PMID 30611954). 39 adults (27 TBI, 12 spontaneous haemorrhage) = 13% of 298
hydrocephalus cases at a Shanghai emergency centre, 2013–18; ventricular
pressure < 70 mm H₂O in all, 8 at ≤ 0 (four at −10 cm H₂O); ~3.5 operations
each; onset-to-final-shunt mean 376 d (31–3880). CNS infection 18/39 (46%),
87.5% in NegPH vs 35% in LPH (P = 0.015); 8 deaths, 6 from infection; NegPH
mortality 5/8 vs 3/29; mean GOS-E 2.7 (1.6 NegPH vs 3.0 LPH). Attributes
infection to prolonged drainage with atmospheric backflow at negative pressure,
and infection/blood to arachnoid adhesion causing the transmantle gradient.
Proposes diagnostic criteria (history, deterioration, CT "ball sign" of the
fourth ventricle, effaced convexity/Sylvian/ambient cisterns, pressure < 70 mm
H₂O) and a classification (high > 200, normal 70–200, low 0–70, negative ≤ 0
mm H₂O). Management is descriptive, not a protocol: "precise CSF external
drainage even at a subzero level", neck wrapping/bellyband/Trendelenburg,
nimodipine, VP shunt once pressure recovers and CSF is sterile in all
compartments, no anti-siphon device, no LP shunt if craniocervical cistern
effaced, and reservoir pumping hundreds of times a day for persistent
ventriculomegaly.

**Diaz-Romero Paz et al. 2019** — *Negative-pressure hydrocephalus: a therapeutic
challenge* (PMID 30710718). ICP −4 cm H₂O after external drainage of a cyst;
removal of the sink plus sub-zero EVD; transmantle-gradient discussion.

**Funnell et al. 2020** — *The ultra-low-pressure hydrocephalic state in NPH:
improvement after shunt siphoning* (Acta Neurochir; PMID 32989519). Shunted
iNPH patients who relapsed with large ventricles at very low ICP and improved
when the valve was reset to allow siphoning; defines the NPH overlap.

**Vilela et al. 2020** (FT) — *Low-pressure hydrocephalus after lumbar puncture in
an adult* (PMID 32712403). Enlarged perimedullary cisterns and brain-stem
distortion; epidural blood patch curative; venous overdrainage discussion.

**Keough, Isaacs, Urbaneja, Hamilton et al. 2021** — *Acute low-pressure
hydrocephalus: a case series and systematic review of 195 patients* (J Neurosurg;
PMID 32736355). 42 local + 153 literature; 53 children, 142 adults; decreased LOC
predominant; neoplasm and haemorrhage the commonest etiologies; 39 % of children
post-LP; shunt in situ 92 % children / 39 % adults; sub-atmospheric drainage the
main temporising step; shunt or ETV definitive; mortality 11 %; return to
baseline 83 % children / 49 % adults.

**Weisbrod et al. 2021** (FT) — *Angiogram-negative SAH and low-pressure
hydrocephalus after COVID-19* (PMID 34462697). Single case; adds a
systemic-inflammatory trigger.

**Casado Pellejero et al. 2022** — *Acute negative-pressure hydrocephalus:
management algorithm and value of early endoscopic third ventriculostomy* (World
Neurosurg; PMID 34998487). 5 patients; algorithm with early ETV applied in 4;
ETV alone succeeded in 2 (50 %), 2 needed shunts; 1 death from systemic
infection; 80 % good outcome.

**Czorlich et al. 2023** — *Acute low-pressure hydrocephalus in aneurysmal SAH*
(PMID 37004138). 15/406 (3.7 %); onset 13.1 ± 7.7 days; IVH presence/extent
associated; aLPH patients went on to chronic hydrocephalus and shunting far more
often than other SAH patients.

**Godoy Hurtado et al. 2023** (FT) — *Low- and negative-pressure hydrocephalus:
new report of six cases and literature review* (J Clin Med; PMID 37373809;
PMC10299038). Six cases (medulloblastoma ×2, TBI with bifrontal craniectomy,
craniopharyngioma, leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour, shunted NPH); ~200 cases
in literature; symptoms follow ventricular size not pressure; sub-zero drainage
most used; neck wrapping, ETV, blood patch as alternatives; pathophysiology
"not clear" — permeability/viscoelasticity changes plus craniospinal SAS
imbalance.

**Zheng et al. 2023** — *Hydrocephalus in severe disorders of consciousness* (PMID
36994490). 68 DOC patients with ventriculomegaly; 60.3 % (41/68) had LPH/NegPH;
45.5 % had one-stage VP shunt + cranioplasty; individualised low valve pressure
by ventricular size and consciousness scores.

**Duan & Hu 2024** — *Low-pressure hydrocephalus: a narrative review* (PMID
38579413). Proposes criteria (Evans > 0.3, ICP ≤ 5 cm H₂O, response to
negative-pressure drainage, exclusion of neurodegeneration); risk factors
include prior radiotherapy, infection, haemorrhage, multiple surgeries; treatment
ladder EVD → ETV/valveless shunt.

**Li et al. 2024** — *Low/negative-pressure hydrocephalus: a review* (PMID
38688300). Four mechanisms (transcortical pressure difference, venous
overdrainage, viscoelastic change, porous elastic sponge); EVD/lumbar-cisternal
drainage first, ETV or shunt definitive.

**Wang et al. 2024** — *Quantitative EEG as early warning in post-SAH acute
low-pressure hydrocephalus* (PMID 39740216). qEEG slowing preceded clinical
deterioration and reversed with CSF removal.

**Kuppler et al. 2025** (FT) — *Chronic negative-pressure hydrocephalus after
failure of prolonged drainage* (PMID 40030163; PMC11877371). Refractory to
low-gradient shunt, neck wrapping, ETV and prolonged sub-atmospheric EVD;
scheduled intermittent active reservoir pressing enabled outpatient management;
defines cNegPH.

**Salam et al. 2025** (FT) — *Theophylline for refractory acute negative-pressure
hydrocephalus* (PMID 40418891; PMC12105587). TBI, hemicraniectomy, shunt
infection, IVH; ICP −5 to +10 mm Hg (nadir −21) despite ~4 months of sub-zero
EVD (to −30 cm H₂O), two ETVs and ventriculopleural/ventriculoatrial shunts;
two doses of theophylline 200 mg via PEG followed by spontaneous drainage,
slit-like ventricles on CT at 4 h and sustained improvement; status epilepticus
as complication. Single case.

**Chen, Li et al. 2025** (FT) — *Low- and negative-pressure hydrocephalus in
children: a systematic analysis of 44 literature cases and 4 institutional
cases* (PMID 40538927; PMC12176887). Craniotomy (mostly posterior-fossa tumour)
the leading antecedent; > 50 % prior surgery; fatigue, vomiting, headache,
bradycardia, seizures, failure to thrive; mean external drainage 41.9 days (2–365);
conservative measures (posture, reservoir pumping, valve adjustment) help a
minority; 90.9 % need shunt repositioning; 77.5 % recover to baseline; poor
outcomes track underlying disease.

**Datta & Tu 2025** — *Pediatric low-pressure hydrocephalus: a case series and
re-analysis of a rare disease* (PMID 41191101). 6 children, ICP ≤ 5 cm H₂O;
low-resistance VP shunts (3) or negative-pressure cavities (3); prior
jugular/sigmoid sinus thrombosis in 2/6; venous-thrombosis model.

**Villalonga et al. 2025** — *ETV plus valveless VP shunt hybrid for LPH* (PMID
41165379). 16 adults meeting Pang–Altschuler criteria; mean KPS gain 56; 81 %
excellent, 19 % temporary improvement; 19 % needed a valved shunt.

**Carrera et al. 2025** — caudal (infraclavicular) programmable valve placement to
exploit the hydrostatic column, 3 patients after prolonged sub-zero drainage (PMID 39951714).

**Chinese Neuroscience Society / Neurosurgical Branch 2025** — *Expert consensus
on diagnosis and treatment of low-pressure hydrocephalus* (PMID 40734409).
Definition (< 70 mm H₂O, progressive ventriculomegaly, worsening deficits),
imaging criteria (effaced Sylvian/convexity SAS, fourth-ventricle "ball sign"),
candidate mechanisms (fourth-ventricular outlet obstruction, compliance
change), management recommendations.

**Bakmeedeniya et al. 2026** — *Management of low/negative pressure hydrocephalus:
a systematic review of etiology, pathophysiology and management* (PMID
41525875). 30 studies, 215 patients (1980–2024); four interacting mechanistic
models; management centred on sub-atmospheric EVD, low-pressure/valveless
shunts, ETV; proposes a standardised diagnostic and management framework;
prognosis governed by etiology and timely recognition.

**Bateman & Bateman 2026** (FT) — *Pathophysiology of sinking flap syndrome
associated with low-pressure hydrocephalus* (PMID 42355921). Phase-contrast MRI:
bilaterally reduced CBF rising 26 % after cranioplasty; reversed aqueductal flow toward
ventricles during LPH; lumped-parameter model favours autoregulatory reset over
venous compression; hypothesises capillary CSF absorption at low ICP.

**Bruk et al. 2026** (FT) — *Neck wrapping for paediatric low-pressure
hydrocephalus* (PMID 42732439). Two children; third ventricle 13 → 8 mm and 13 →
4 mm; both internalised afterwards.

**Hoffman et al. 2026** (FT) — *Post-LP low-pressure hydrocephalus in a shunted
adult* (PMID 42224725). Diagnostic sequence: shunt-tap manometry, patency
confirmation, imaging for sink and block; treated with drainage and blood patch.

### C. Mechanistic and modelling anchors from the supporting axes

- Sklar 1980 brain elasticity changes with ventriculomegaly (PMID 6893601);
  Shapiro 1987 no transmantle gradient in cats (PMID 3598675); Conner 1984
  gradient in experimental NPH (PMID 6737056); Stephensen 2002 no gradient in
  communicating hydrocephalus (PMID 11904027); Eide & Saehle 2010 pulsatile
  gradient (PMID 20130957).
- Czosnyka 1996/2001 pressure–volume compensation (PMIDs 8778261, 11235954);
  Kim 2009 compensatory reserve (PMID 19240611); Gholampour 2022 compliance
  after shunting (PMID 35979170).
- Peña 1999, Dutta-Roy 2008, Chou 2016, Kim 2016 poroelastic FE models (PMIDs
  10414573, 18534602, 26671218, 26274984); Solamen 2021 poroelastic MRE in NPH
  (PMID 32331966); Duy 2024 brain–CSF interface instability (PMID 38798141).
- Bateman 2002/2008 pulse-wave encephalopathy (PMIDs 12221445, 18379767); Egnor
  2023/2026 windkessel impedance classification (PMIDs 37382303, 41791099);
  Nozaleda 2025 pulsation-driven glymphatic flow (PMID 40258946).
- Hatt 2015 jugular compression stiffens brain on MRE (PMID 26045579); Sainz 2019
  venous hypertension and turgor (PMID 30474714); Shulyakov 2011/2012 and Jugé
  2016 animal viscoelasticity (PMIDs 21316637, 22806081, 26848844); Wagshul 2021
  reduced white-matter stiffness in early hydrocephalus (PMID 33631603);
  Dirrichs 2019 infant shear-wave elastography (PMID 31464808); Rekate 2020
  infant compliance (PMID 32488353).
- Raimondi 1994 unifying theory (PMID 8194058); Oi 2011 multi-categorical
  classification (PMID 21928018); Orešković & Klarica 2011 bulk-flow critique
  (PMID 21641963); Bergsneider, Egnor et al. 2006 *What we don't (but should)
  know about hydrocephalus* (PMID 16572631).
